Most say they were over 18 when they interacted with Walliams. The allegations extend to his conduct in professional environments, with “several sources” describing inappropriate behavior toward women on both Britain‘s Got Talent and his publisher, HarperCollins.

The investigation follows a slew of news stories that have emerged on his behavior in recent years, including his being completely dropped by HarperCollins in 2025. Walliams is one of the country’s best-selling authors, having sold over 50 to 60 million copies of his books worldwide, with Gangsta Granny, Mr. Stink and The Boy in the Dress among his most famous.

But a report in The Daily Telegraph in December 2025 accused Walliams of “harassing” junior female employees at HarperCollins, where former staff said they were told to work in “pairs” when meeting him and advised not to visit his home. He strongly denied the claims at the time.

TMZ recently reported that Walliams had been dropped from an upcoming film, The Road to Nevermore, as allegations of misconduct surfaced. It is unclear if these allegations are connected to the claims made in The Guardian and ITV News.

Then last week came the sudden closure of The World of David Walliams, an attraction at one of the U.K.’s flagship theme parks, Alton Towers. The Merlin Entertainments-owned park said it would permanently close the area, which brought to life the characters from Walliams’ massively popular books, after five years.

“As the 2026 peak season at Alton Towers Resort comes to an end and following our regular review of rides and attractions across the resort, we have taken the decision to permanently close the World of David Walliams,” said a Merlin spokesperson to THR. The spokesperson declined to elaborate but said a range of operational and guest experience decisions were taken into account.

In June last year, Walliams drew widespread condemnation, including from the BBC, for making two Nazi salutes during a recording of the British panel show Would I Lie To You?. He reportedly made the gestures during a segment in which another panellist joked about injuring their wrist while waving. The audience at Pinewood Studios, where the show’s Christmas special was filmed, was reportedly shocked when Walliams joined in to mimic the waves before holding his arm in a Nazi salute.

Life can leave its mark on a planetary atmosphere, so learning what properties are the product of non-life will help astronomers identify those worlds that might have life.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A new computer simulation that depicts Earth, or a rocky planet in general, without life is the latest tool in the quest to discover whether or not we are alone in the universe.

Life leaves its mark on a planet, particularly its atmosphere, in the form of a mixture of biochemically created gases. Some are obvious, while others can be produced by both biology and geology, meaning that distinguishing a planet that has life from one that does not, solely based on what gases we can detect in its atmosphere, can be difficult. The key is in knowing which atmospheric conditions can be explained without life.

To aid in distinguishing between habitable and inhabited planets, planetary scientist Samantha Gilbert-Janizek of the University of California, Riverside, developed a model that simulates the evolution of a rocky planet without life.

"The model can help us see how habitable but non-living planets might mimic living planets," Gilbert-Janizek, who was a PhD student at the University of Washington when the research was conducted, said in a statement.

Gilbert-Janizek built upon a model previously developed by Washington’s Rory Barnes that simulated the core, mantle, and crust of a planet. This new model pushed the simulation two steps further by incorporating the surface and atmosphere of the planet as well.

In all, the model simulates 19 properties of a rocky planet that are not related to life, including the amount of heat a planet receives from its star, the exchange of heat and chemicals from the core to the surface, and the outflow of certain gases from the subsurface.

Gilbert-Janizek’s starting point was to simulate the development of Earth had life never arisen here, therefore providing a baseline with which to compare to exoplanets. She ran the simulation from the birth of Earth 4.5 billion years ago to 500 million years into the future. The result was a lifeless world, but one that still had oceans and an atmosphere.

"When we interpret observations of an exoplanet’s atmosphere, this tool will help us determine the probability that what we observe indicates life on the surface," said Gilbert-Janizek.

What makes the simulation especially useful is its plug-and-play nature. Researchers can simply apply the bulk properties of whichever planet they are studying to the model, and then just let it run. If the result is a planet with an atmosphere that matches what is detected spectroscopically by the James Webb Space Telescope or, in the future, the various extremely large 30-meter-plus ground-based telescopes or NASA’s planned Habitable Worlds Observatory, then we know that planet probably does not have life as we know it.

However, if the simulated planet without life does not match what we observe on the real planet, then it becomes possible that life is present and altering the atmosphere.

"Dr Gilbert-Janizek’s work represents an exciting step toward understanding where life can exist in the universe,” said Barnes. "After more than a decade of work by many scientists, Dr Gilbert-Janizek has finally completed a model of the Earth that simultaneously reproduces properties of Earth’s core, mantle, surface and atmosphere. That calibration gives us confidence that future simulations of exoplanets will be accurate."

While any deviation from what is predicted by the model will not necessarily mean there is definitely life on a planet, it will help pick out those worlds that are worthy of follow-up studies by the next generation of telescopes.

Gilbert-Janizek’s model is described in a paper published in The Planetary Science Journal.

Keith Cooper is a freelance science journalist and editor in the United Kingdom, and has a degree in physics and astrophysics from the University of Manchester. He's the author of "The Contact Paradox: Challenging Our Assumptions in the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence" (Bloomsbury Sigma, 2020) and has written articles on astronomy, space, physics and astrobiology for a multitude of magazines and websites.

#751. A hidden star is plowing through Betelgeuse’s atmosphere, new evidence suggests

Something unusual is happening inside the enormous atmosphere of Betelgeuse, one of the most recognizable stars in the night sky. Astronomers have detected subtle changes in the star's shape that suggest something is moving through its outer layers, disturbing the surrounding gas like an unseen visitor making noise inside a house. (Metaphorically speaking.) New observations point to a likely culprit: Siwarha, a recently discovered companion star that appears to be traveling through Betelgeuse's atmosphere.

Betelgeuse is a massive red supergiant located in the constellation Orion, where it forms the famous hunter's shoulder. Although the star has fascinated astronomers for generations, it attracted worldwide attention in late 2019 and early 2020 when its brightness unexpectedly plunged to its lowest recorded level in more than 100 years. The event, known as the Great Dimming, raised questions about what was happening inside the aging star.

Now, observations from the U.S. National Science Foundation's Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array (NSF VLA) and the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) reveal that Betelgeuse's vast outer atmosphere has largely returned to normal. More intriguingly, the measurements provide new evidence that a nearby companion star is physically disturbing the giant star's atmosphere.

The research was led by Dr. Lynn D. Matthews, Principal Research Scientist and Assistant Director at MIT Haystack Observatory, working with scientists from the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian, the University of Manchester, and the European Southern Observatory. The team analyzed observations gathered between 2021 and 2026 at seven radio frequencies ranging from 22 GHz to 485 GHz.

Different radio frequencies allow astronomers to examine different depths within a star's atmosphere. By combining the observations from both telescopes, the researchers reconstructed the structure of Betelgeuse's outer layers, beginning just above its visible surface and extending outward to several times its radius.

"It was the combination of the incredible data from the NSF VLA and ALMA that gave us a convincing result here," said Matthews. "The fact that we can use these facilities to actually resolve the disks of nearby stars is amazing."

Betelgeuse Recovers From Its Mysterious Great Dimming

The latest measurements also help scientists understand how Betelgeuse has changed since its extraordinary fading episode. Several months before the Great Dimming (when Betelgeuse ejected a billion tons of solar material, partially blocking our view), an earlier investigation led by Matthews detected unusually low temperatures in the star's atmosphere at radio wavelengths.

At the time, researchers suggested that turbulent convection deep inside Betelgeuse may have generated a shock wave that traveled outward and disrupted the surrounding gas. That disturbance could have helped trigger the enormous release of material that later formed dust and obscured part of the star's light.

The new observations indicate that the atmosphere has since warmed to temperatures more typical of Betelgeuse. At a distance of approximately 2.7 times the star's radius, the gas now has a measured brightness temperature of about 3,500 Kelvin (comparable to Betelgeuse's own surface temperature).

Astronomers Discover an Unexpectedly Cold Atmospheric Layer

The researchers also confirmed a feature that scientists had suspected existed for years: a region of unusually cool gas between Betelgeuse's visible surface and its higher atmospheric layer, known as the chromosphere.

Using ALMA at its highest observed frequencies, the team was able to probe closer to the star's surface than previous radio measurements had allowed. The results revealed temperatures falling to approximately 2,200 Kelvin, more than 1,000 degrees below the temperature of the visible surface, or photosphere.

This cool region corresponds to the "MOLsphere," a layer containing molecular gas that astronomers had previously identified primarily through infrared observations. The new radio measurements provide a much more direct examination of this elusive part of Betelgeuse's atmosphere and confirm the long-suspected "temperature minimum."

A Hidden Companion Star May Be Distorting Betelgeuse

One of the most intriguing discoveries involves Siwarha, the smaller star believed to orbit extremely close to Betelgeuse. Astronomers first proposed the companion's existence in 2024 as a possible explanation for a puzzling cycle in which Betelgeuse's brightness changes approximately every 2,100 days. Subsequent direct imaging and spectroscopic observations have provided additional support for the companion's existence.

The name Siwarha reflects its relationship with Betelgeuse. The giant star's name comes from the Arabic expression meaning "the hand of al-Jawza," while Siwarha means "her bracelet."

Unlike a planet or star traveling far from its host, Siwarha is believed to follow an orbit that takes it directly through Betelgeuse's extended atmosphere. Its estimated orbital distance is only about twice the red supergiant's radius.

"This companion is orbiting so close to the star that it actually passes through its extended atmosphere," Matthews explained.

As Siwarha moves along its orbit, it may push through the surrounding gas much like a fast boat cutting through water. The resulting wake could disturb the atmosphere, producing changes that astronomers can detect even though the smaller star itself remains invisible in the radio observations.

In fact, the researchers calculated that Siwarha is likely tens to hundreds of times too faint to be detected directly with the radio measurements they collected. Instead, they searched for indirect evidence of its presence by studying the shape of Betelgeuse's atmosphere.

Betelgeuse's Changing Shape Reveals New Clues

The scientists discovered that Betelgeuse does not always appear perfectly round at radio wavelengths. Its atmosphere sometimes develops a slightly stretched, oval appearance, and the timing of these changes appears to match the expected position of Siwarha.

To investigate this connection, the team measured the atmosphere's departure from a circular shape ("ellipticity") across observations taken at different times.

They found that Betelgeuse tends to look more elongated when Siwarha is expected to be at its greatest apparent separation from the giant star. When the companion is predicted to pass in front of or behind Betelgeuse from our perspective, the atmosphere appears rounder.

This relationship provides compelling evidence that the smaller star may be influencing the shape of Betelgeuse's outer layers through gravity and its physical passage through the gas.

The effect resembles noticing ripples spreading across a pond without being able to see what caused them. Although Siwarha remains too faint to identify directly at radio wavelengths, the changing shape of Betelgeuse's atmosphere may reveal its movement around the larger star.

Future Observations Could Reveal More About Betelgeuse

Despite the promising results, astronomers emphasize that additional observations are necessary to confirm the connection between Siwarha's orbit and the atmospheric distortions. Measurements covering more of the companion's orbital cycle, particularly at radio frequencies that have not yet been studied extensively, could help establish how strongly the smaller star affects Betelgeuse.

More advanced instruments may eventually provide an even clearer picture. The Next Generation Very Large Array, an observatory currently under development, is expected to make detailed studies of nearby stars and their atmospheres much easier.

Such observations could reveal not only how companion stars influence their massive neighbors, but also how aging red supergiants lose material as they approach the final stages of their lives. Understanding these interactions may help astronomers better explain the complicated processes that shape the evolution of enormous stars like Betelgeuse.

The findings were published in The Astronomical Journal in a paper titled "New Spatially Resolved Observations of Betelgeuse from the VLA and ALMA: Evidence for Atmospheric Perturbations from a Close Companion."

#749. British Horror ‘Rise of the Rats,’ Dark-Web Chess Thriller ‘The Rules of the Game’ Head to AFM With Black Mandala, Red Owl (EXCLUSIVE)

Killer rats overrun a village in British horror “Rise of the Rats,” one of eight genre titles that New Zealand sales company Black Mandala and its Red Owl label are taking to the American Film Market (AFM).

Black Mandala is handling four of the films, while Red Owl is bringing four independent features. Between them, the slate covers horror, psychological thriller, supernatural and dark fantasy. Related Stories Lula’s Election Win: How Fan Accounts for Taylor Swift, Billie Eilish and More Helped Him to a Historic Victory and Defeat for Trump Taylor Swift’s Canceled Vienna Concerts Due to Thwarted Terrorist Plot to Be Subject of Documentary

Directed by Stephen Roach, “Rise of the Rats” follows Kayla Thornhill, a punk who travels with the father she is estranged from to Ditchfield, the village where he grew up. The infestation there turns out to conceal something worse, old violence and village secrets resurface, and a figure known as the Rat-Man sets a bloodthirsty swarm loose, leaving Kayla fighting to survive. Grace Gallagher, Adrian Annis and Mark Collier star.

Black Mandala is also handling Remington Smith’s “Landlord,” which plays out over a hot summer in a run-down apartment block. A Black bounty hunter who has come to retrieve a stolen briefcase ends up having to shield a young boy, Alex, from the white vampire who owns the building and so has no need to be invited in. Once the vampire has killed Alex’s mother, the pair team up to take on him and the humans who work for him. Adama Abramson, Cohen James Cooper and William McKinney lead the cast.

Myles McEwen and Ripley Stevens co-direct “Haunted,” set in One Season, a remote Australian town hit by a fierce storm and an event nobody can explain on Oct. 19, 2003. Four years later, local teenagers start going missing, and a recluse whose house is slated for demolition is forced to leave his solitary life behind as a supernatural force pursues him. He has to face a hidden truth connected to the town’s trauma and to who he really is. David Daradan, Joseph Baronio and Nathaniel Kelly star.

Rounding out the Black Mandala titles is Oliver Hollingdale’s dark fantasy “The Realm of Eldervin: Gallowmere,” which Variety previously reported the company had acquired. A strange illness caused by dark magic has struck Gallowmere, a village in the woods of Eldervin, and Jonas the Mage puts together a band made up of Dagon, Nimue and Solomon to trace its origin. Their quest pulls them into a bleak world where a second chance always comes at a cost. Martin Portlock and Craig Standen star, with Jason Flemyng (“Lock, Stock and Two Smoking Barrels”) providing voiceover narration.

On the Red Owl side, Lani Castle and Jon Cohen’s psychological thriller “The Rules of the Game” centers on Evie, a gifted chess player who is abducted along with her sister, who has a chronic illness, and forced into a lethal game streamed on the dark web. She and seven other prisoners each stand in for a chess piece, and any piece that is taken is killed. Evie is the only one who knows how the game works, and she has to make agonizing calls as the others turn on one another. Lola Merewether, Gezel Bardossi and Alyson Rudlin star.

Chad Costen’s horror-comedy “Mister Sandman” sees a group of onetime summer camp outcasts reunite at a deserted camp to dig into a ghost story they all recall. Each of them, working through grief’s five stages, must face a personal fear that surfaces as a nightmarish vision linked to an old trauma. Elodie Doumenc, Justine Warrington and Amy King star.

Daniel Lerch’s “Saturnalia,” a homage to Italian giallo, is set in 1979. After her parents die in mysterious circumstances, Miriam Basconi is enrolled at Alstroemerias Academy, an elite school run by the cruel Headmistress Hemlock, where pupils disappear after dark and strange men lurk. Her investigation uncovers a surreal hidden world inside the school, where dreams and waking life have started to blur. Sophia Anthony, Velvet and Dante Blake star.

Tim Connery’s anthology “The Driftless” draws on the folklore of the American Midwest. An enigmatic antique dealer introduces four stories: cults along the Mississippi River, a musician and a bottle of liquor that carries a curse, a motel pool attendant who recovers objects that alter time and a woman who takes bloody revenge after death. Ira Amyx, Torrey Hanson and Justin Marxen star.

Black Mandala has built an international profile as a sales outfit devoted to horror and genre fare, and Red Owl extends that remit to independent titles with distinctive premises. Teams from both banners plan to meet buyers, distributors, platforms and festivals at AFM.

The three-headed Kaiju's origins aren't just space-based; one of the largest structures in the universe shares its name.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Godzilla goes toe-to-toe with long-time foe King Ghidorah in Godzilla Minus Zero, which opened in theaters on Friday (Nov. 6). Though the three-headed golden Kaiju might seem like a natural native of Monster Island, King Ghidorah actually emerged from the depths of space.

However, it isn't just the origins of King Ghidorah — also known as Monster Zero in the Godzilla movie Invasion of Astro-Monster (1965) — that are this beast's only cosmic connection. One of the largest structures in the universe, the King Ghidorah Supercluster, was named in honor of Godzilla's primary antagonist.

King Ghidorah is a three-headed, twin-tailed golden dragon from the stars, first introduced in the fifth Godzilla movie, Ghidorah, the Three-Headed Monster (1964).

In this first appearance, part of the Shōwa era (1964–1975) of Godzilla history, Ghidorah ravaged Venus, wiping out its population 5,000 years before arriving on Earth encased within a highly magnetic meteorite. Ghidorah was bested this first time by Godzilla, Rodan, and Mothra.

Undeterred, Ghidorah returned for a rematch just a year later in Invasion of Astro Monster (1965), after being discovered supposedly terrorizing the inhabitants of Planet X, a world found beyond Jupiter. In this movie, it is revealed that Ghidorah is less a king and more a pawn, under the control of calculating Xiliens as part of a plan to subjugate Earth. This will become a theme.

Freed from that control, Ghidorah returns to deep space, once again falling under the thrall of an alien race in 1968's Destroy All Monsters.This movie sees Ghidorah hold its own against a who's who of kaiju, eventually succumbing to the combined might of Godzilla, Minilla, Mothra, Rodan, Manda, Gorosaurus, Anguirus, Kumonga, Baragon, and Varan.

Even with three gravity-beam-blasting heads, that is hardly fair!

Ghidorah returned with some backup for a final time in the Shōwa era in 1975's Godzilla vs. Gigan. This time, Ghidorah and his tag-team partner Gigan (who resembled a giant one-eyed space chicken) were under the control of cockroach-like Nebulans. Getting mind-controlled three times is just embarrassing!

Fortunately, the Shōwa era drew to a close in 1975 before Ghidorah was forced into servitude for a fourth time.

Ghidorah returned in the rebooted Godzilla timeline of the Heisei era (1991–1998) in 1991's Godzilla Vs. King Ghidorah, but its cosmic origins are gone. The Heisei Ghidorah begins life as three genetically engineered creatures called Dorats in the future before being morphed into a three-headed form via nuclear exposure.

Ghidorah was given a spiritual origin in the Millennium era's Godzilla, Mothra, and King Ghidorah: Giant Monsters All-Out Attack (2001), actually serving as a protagonist, helping Mothra in halting Godzilla's rampage.

Ghidorah is once again an extraterrestrial in Universal Pictures' MonsterVerse movie Godzilla: King of the Monsters (2019), being described as having "fallen from the stars" in ancient times before rising to challenge Godzilla.

Now King Ghidorah is back once again in Godzilla Minus Zero, maintaining his extraterrestrial origin story and once again challenging Godzilla to an epic kaiju battle. Those are some of the fictional versions of this golden beast, but what does it look like in reality?

Arguably the most impressive feat of King Ghidorah has been to make itself such an important part of pop culture that astronomers took note. The King Ghidorah supercluster is a collection of galaxies located around 6.7 billion light-years from Earth. Covering an area of the sky equivalent to 19 full moons, as seen from our vantage point, this cosmic Kaiju was discovered in late 2022 by Japanese astronomers using data from the Subaru Telescope.

The King Ghidorah supercluster is comprised of at least 19 individual associated galaxy clusters. It stretches out for an incredible 1.3 billion light-years, meaning the entire Milky Way could fit across it around 12,300 times. That makes it the largest supercluster ever discovered.

To put into context just how monstrous the King Ghidorah supercluster is, consider the fact that it has a mass equivalent to 10,000,000,000,000,000 suns, 10 times as massive as the Milky Way's home supercluster, Laniakea. Even Godzilla may think twice before attempting to tussle with that particular King Ghidorah!

See King Ghidorah in action in Godzilla Minus Zero, which is showing in theaters in the US and UK from November 6. You can see the preceding movie, Godzilla Minus One, on Netflix.

#747. NASA smashed into an asteroid. Now Hera is closing in to see what happened

The European Space Agency's Hera spacecraft has reached an important milestone in its mission to investigate a historic asteroid collision. For the first time, its onboard camera has captured the two asteroids Didymos and Dimorphos as separate objects rather than a single point of light.

The asteroid pair is currently about 197 million kilometers from Earth. Hera obtained the new image on the evening of October 18 using its black-and-white Asteroid Framing Camera, while the spacecraft was approximately 1,280 kilometers from its targets.

"With this image, the smaller Dimorphos asteroid becomes visible for the first time," explains Michael Kueppers. "Before this acquisition, the spacecraft was still resolving the Didymos system as a single dot. But now, even though Dimorphos is made up of only around one pixel in this initial image, it is clearly well separated from its parent body."

The breakthrough image follows a successful series of maneuvers designed to slow Hera as it approaches the asteroid system. Earlier in October, the spacecraft fired its thrusters twice, with one week between the maneuvers. These adjustments reduced its speed relative to the asteroids to just 20 meters per second, allowing mission controllers to carefully manage the remaining approach.

Although the two asteroids appear tiny in the initial image, they are substantial objects. Dimorphos measures about 151 meters across, making it roughly comparable in size to the Great Pyramid of Giza. Its larger companion, Didymos, is approximately 780 meters in diameter, slightly smaller than the height of Dubai's Burj Khalifa, the world's tallest building.

Dimorphos travels around Didymos at an average separation of just 1.15 kilometers, moving at a speed of approximately 18 centimeters per second.

"For the very first time we are seeing through Hera's own eyes the very double asteroid system that the mission was designed and built for," adds mission manager Ian Carnelli.

"Our views will grow much sharper as Hera comes closer. We will unveil the first detailed images of Dimorphos -- the first object in the Solar System to have had its orbit measurably shifted by human action -- on 25 November."

Uncovering the Aftermath of NASA's Historic Asteroid Collision

Hera's arrival will give scientists an opportunity to examine the results of a groundbreaking planetary defense experiment conducted four years earlier.

On September 26, 2022, NASA's Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) spacecraft deliberately collided with Dimorphos at approximately 6.1 kilometers per second. The impact blasted debris as far as 10,000 kilometers into space and shortened the asteroid's orbital period around Didymos by roughly 33 minutes.

The experiment demonstrated that a spacecraft could deliberately change an asteroid's motion, an achievement with potentially enormous implications for protecting Earth from future asteroid threats.

However, the collision also produced results that scientists are still trying to fully explain. The asteroid's orbital change was substantially greater than computer simulations had predicted, raising questions about its physical properties and how it responded to the impact.

Researchers still do not know whether DART left a crater on Dimorphos or significantly altered the asteroid's overall shape. They also need more precise measurements of its composition, internal structure, and mass to understand why the collision was so effective.

Answering these questions is essential for transforming the 'kinetic impact' approach into a reliable planetary defense strategy.

Hera Prepares for a Detailed Asteroid Investigation

Over the coming months, Hera will carry out a detailed 'crash site investigation' to uncover what NASA's collision actually did to Dimorphos.

The spacecraft will use a collection of scientific instruments to examine the asteroid and its surroundings. It will also release two small satellites, known as 'CubeSats', each approximately the size of a shoebox, to gather additional observations from much closer distances. The investigation is expected to eventually include landing operations.

Together, these measurements should help scientists better understand how asteroids respond to high-speed impacts and improve predictions of how future deflection attempts might work.

Anyone interested in following Hera's journey can explore the mission through the Hera Space Companion. More than a conventional AI chatbot, this interactive communication platform is connected to the mission and designed to make the European Space Agency's first planetary defense mission accessible to the public.

#746. Why your physics project needs an anthropologist

Jaco de Swart is a historian and anthropologist of science at the University of Cambridge, UK.

The TAMBO team assesses suitable observatory sites in the Andes Mountains of Peru.Credit: Jaco de Swart

It is uncommon for a social scientist to have a seat at a meeting about an astronomical observatory, let alone for them to jointly lead one. For one-quarter of attendees to be social-science scholars is almost unprecedented. But that’s exactly what happens at meetings about the Tau Air-shower Mountain-based Observatory (TAMBO), a proposed detector to be built in the Peruvian Andes to look for cosmic particles called tau neutrinos.

Space diplomacy: bridging the operating gaps between myriad missions

Space diplomacy: bridging the operating gaps between myriad missions

Tau neutrinos are elusive fundamental particles that are transmitted through space from black holes and other distant sources. When these particles interact with rocks on Earth, they can produce a shower of other, short-lived particles. The idea behind TAMBO is that if such a shower were emitted from one side of a deep canyon, it could be picked up by an array of 5,000 detectors on the other side (TAMBO collaboration. Nature Astron. 10, 947–951; 2026). The Andes Mountains of Peru contain many promising sites.

For those who live in the area, however, the case for TAMBO is less clear. The Andes are a sensitive ecological environment and home to Indigenous farming communities that consider the mountains sentient beings that are integral to their society. The area is also affected by legal and illegal mining, large-scale infrastructure projects and legacies of colonialism. This all leads to scepticism towards large projects that are developed by people from outside the area.

I am the co-principal investigator of the TAMBO collaboration, alongside Peruvian neutrino physicist Carlos Argüelles at Harvard University in Cambridge, Massachusetts. I lead the social-science and ‘responsible siting’ side of the project. Having received funding to build a proof-of-principle experiment called TAMBITO, we are searching for a potential location for the observatory.

Developing astronomers in Africa: ‘We wanted to create a discipline’

Developing astronomers in Africa: ‘We wanted to create a discipline’

Since 2024, the TAMBO collaboration has built partnerships with 11 Peruvian institutions, which are involved in the design and development of the telescope. Scientific links are an important starting point, but they are not enough. No matter what their discovery potential is, big scientific experiments are not beneficial to everyone. For example, construction of the Thirty Meter Telescope has been stalled since 2015 because of protests triggered by objections to its planned site on Maunakea in Hawaii — a mountain that is sacred in Native Hawaiian culture.

To integrate environmental care into the project and build good relationships with the communities that might host the telescope, TAMBO brought in experts on the Andean region. In 2024, the collaboration held a workshop at Harvard’s Radcliffe Institute for Advanced Study, at which scholars and policymakers discussed what equitable astrophysics in Peru would look like. This led to the formation of a responsible-siting team that includes geographers, sociologists and anthropologists who have worked in the Andes.

#745. Lana Condor, Anthony De La Torre Team for Rom-Com Microseries for Fetch (Exclusive)

Digital creator Eric Sedeño also stars in ‘The Receipt,’ a six-part ultrashort comedy to premiere Dec. 3.

Rom-com queen Lana Condor and husband Anthony De La Torre are set to star in The Receipt, a six-part holiday-themed microseries with brand partnerships from Fetch, the rewards app.

All the Boys I’ve Loved Before star Condor will play Chloe who after a holiday tote bag mix-up has to find Max, a mysterious stranger, with the help of Liam, her best friend played by digital content maker Eric Sedeño. Chloe begins piecing together Max’s identity via clues from his everyday purchases.

“We wanted to make something people would genuinely want to watch, not something that felt like an ad they had to sit through. The Receipt has all the ingredients of a classic holiday rom-com – a missed connection, a little mystery, and a love story you want to root for. Think Cinderella meets Hallmark, but told in short episodes designed for the way people watch today. And because it’s Fetch, we’re giving audiences a way to get rewarded along the way,” Spychalski said in a statement.

The holiday romancer will launch on the Fetch app and social media platforms and will see brand partners including Dove, Betty Crocker and Breyers woven into storylines for episodes each to last two to four minutes.

That will allow viewers of the ultrashort comedy product offers and rewards via the Fetch app. They will earn Fetch Points by watching episode clips in the app and making qualifying purchases of featured products, before then redeeming points for gift cards.

The Receipt promises a new branded entertainment model for how marketers, content creators and the traditional entertainment industry can work together, Spychalski added.

“It’s no longer enough to put your product in a scene and hope people notice. The opportunity is to help create something audiences actually care about. With The Receipt, brands like Dove, Betty Crocker and Breyers are woven authentically into the story itself, and Fetch extends that connection beyond the screen and into the shopping experiences people have every day. That’s a much more interesting relationship that drives real outcomes between a brand and its audience,” he argued.

The Receipt also looks to leverage industry trends towards the emergence of social-first scripted content, digital creators and influencers and major brands investing in entertainment to reach consumers.

Sedeño explained co-starring in The Receipt is part of the creator economy emerging from YouTube and other online platforms drawing eyeballs form traditional linear TV channels and streamers.

“What’s really exciting to me is how much the world is opening up for creators. We’re not just making sponsored posts. We’re getting opportunities to act, tell bigger stories, and work with incredible talent. I love that Fetch didn’t just bring creators in to help promote a show. They actually made us part of the entertainment. That’s a pretty exciting evolution, and I think we’re going to see a lot more of it,” Sedeño said in his own statement.

After the launch episode, fresh ones will debut every 72 hours through Dec. 18. Fetch as a rewards app for consumers and brands allows users to earn points from everyday activities, including shopping, dining out or playing mobile games. Over $100 million in rewards will be redeemed from Fetch this holiday season, the company said.

#744. Phil Rosenthal’s ‘Somebody Feeds Phil’ Flies to YouTube From Netflix, With Lift From United

Phil Rosenthal’s food-focused travelogue show is moving from Netflix to YouTube — and United Airlines helped the writer and host make the journey.

“Somebody Feed Phil” has streamed on Netflix for eight seasons, and Rosenthal says he realized the series’ time on the service was coming to an end. Thanks to a new pact with Banijay Entertainment, the program will continue on the Alphabet streaming giant, where it can be seen for free — along with some sponsorships that help Rosenthal keep on traveling. United is the title sponsor of the series’ ninth season, and will offer the new cycle on its seatback entertainment system on its flights. Viewers will also see United Airlines woven into some scenes in the series next eight-episode flight.

“They help us with the crew, with the equipment, and we avoid all the hassle of landing with tons of equipment in foreign countries,” explains Rosenthal, creator of the popular comedy “Everybody Loves Raymond.” “It’s a natural relationship because we are both interested in travel.”

And yet, United’s decision to link itself to the series shows the airline looking to stand out from the usual marketing flyover. In a different era, many airlines ran TV commercials regularly and burnished slogans like “We love to fly and it shows,” “Fly the friendly skies” and “Fly smart.” In an era filled with websites that seek out the exact fares, prices and schedules consumers are seeking, brand image has taken a back seat to the consumer’s travel needs. By embracing Rosenthal’s show, United hopes to show customers current and future that its flights can do more than just satisfy a basic need.

Having “Somebody Feed Phil” available to flyers gives United a chance to inspire travelers to visit places via its own routes, says Maggie Schmerin, United’s chief advertising officer, during a recent interview. Flyers can “use their time in air “ to “get an idea of where do I want to go on my next trip,” she says. “We have such a captive audience on board” and some kinds of content can help to underscore the airline’s vast route network.

As part of its sponsorship, United will offer MileagePlus loyalty members a chance to win flights and meet Rosenthal. Fans can visit http://www.somebodyfindphil.com and guess the cities that will be featured in the show’s upcoming season. For every correct guess, participants are entered for a chance to win a roundtrip flight for two, in any class of service, to their choice of one of the eight cities featured in Season 9. United will give away eight pairs of tickets throughout the month of December, and will also draw one grand prize winner that includes a roundtrip flight for two, in any class of service, to one city featured in Season 9, plus a meal with Phil at his Los Angeles diner Max & Helen’s.

The move to YouTube from Netflix opens the chance to reach a significantly wider audience, Rosenthal says, but to do so, he thinks he will need help. “There are billions of choices on YouTube. So, obviously, you want to stand out from the crowd. Otherwise, you’re just lost in a sea of content,” Rosenthal says. He expects to do more than just stream a series, including, potentially, building out microdramas or other kinds of short-form content. He can also do specific pieces of content for sponsors.

United is doing more to woo interest via social media, says Schmerin, including tapping members of its employee base who have cultivated followings on various platforms or working with outside influencers who discuss travel.

The company sees a chance for a longer-term alliance with Rosenthal says the executive. “It feels like as long as there are places to explore, it’s a show that could have a lot of value.”

#743. Permanent daylight saving time has a dark side, scientists warn

Keeping daylight saving time in effect all year could bring brighter evenings, but new research suggests the change would come with a troubling consequence for American children. A nationwide switch could result in at least 2 billion additional trips to school in darkness, potentially increasing safety risks while reducing children's exposure to important morning sunlight.

The debate over permanent daylight saving time has gained momentum in Washington, D.C. This past summer, the U.S. House of Representatives approved legislation that would eliminate the annual return to standard time in the fall. Nineteen states, including Washington, have already approved measures supporting the change, which would take effect in those states if the federal bill becomes law.

The legislation remains stalled in the Senate, with school start times emerging as a major concern. Permanent daylight saving time (DST) would push sunrise an hour later during the winter months, leaving mornings darker from November through March. Although this would affect everyone traveling early in the day, researchers at the University of Washington wanted to understand what it would mean specifically for children heading to school.

Permanent Daylight Saving Time Could Add Billions of Dark School Commutes

To measure the potential impact, the research team examined 14 of the 19 states that have already approved permanent daylight saving time measures. They combined school enrollment figures, individual school start times, and geographic coordinates to determine how frequently students would need to travel to school before sunrise. The researchers then calculated the total number of these trips under the proposed system and compared it with the current practice of changing clocks twice a year.

The results revealed substantial increases. In Washington state alone, permanent daylight saving time would produce nearly 35 million additional school commutes in darkness. Similar patterns emerged across the other 13 states, with Georgia showing the largest increase at approximately 71 million additional dark trips.

When the researchers extended their findings to estimate the nationwide impact, they calculated that permanent daylight saving time would create at least 2 billion more trips to school before sunrise compared with the current system.

The potential consequences go beyond inconvenient mornings. An analysis of U.S. traffic collision records found that fatal crashes involving school-aged pedestrians were roughly twice as likely to occur during dark mornings as after sunrise. The findings were published October 29 in the journal Current Biology.

"It's called the 'Sunshine Protection Act' because you get an extra hour of light at the end of the day. But you will take that hour from the morning. You could call it the Sunshine Destruction Act," said senior author Horacio de la Iglesia, a professor of biology at the University of Washington. "These dark mornings will inequitably affect children who have to go to school at a certain time. It's a very tangible metric that anybody from any state or socioeconomic background can relate to. Nobody wants their kids to go to school in the dark."

Why Morning Sunlight Matters for Children's Health

Beyond concerns about traffic safety, losing access to morning sunlight could interfere with the body's natural daily rhythms. Bright light early in the day helps synchronize the circadian clock, the internal timing system that influences sleep, mood, appetite, and other important functions. When people receive too little morning light, maintaining these biological rhythms can become more difficult.

For children, who must typically follow fixed school schedules, darker mornings could mean missing a valuable opportunity to receive daylight at a time when their bodies need it.

"When we send kids to school in the dark, we are depriving them from an opportunity to get that morning daylight," said lead author Guadalupe Rodríguez Ferrante, a postdoctoral researcher in biology at the University of Washington. "We were asking what's the cost for these children. We wanted actual numbers, a real number of kids based on the geographic location of each school."

The researchers also identified which communities would experience the greatest changes. Schools located near the western boundaries of time zones, including those in Forks, Washington, would be particularly affected because sunrise already occurs relatively late in those locations. Districts that begin classes early in the morning would face similarly large increases in dark commutes.

Mississippi and Alabama offer striking examples. Schools in both states begin, on average, before 8 a.m. Under the current clock system, each state has approximately 2 million school trips in darkness. With permanent daylight saving time, that figure would rise to more than 20 million trips per state.

"Some districts probably never experience a dark commute under the current system, and, if this passes, suddenly they will wake up to this new reality that their kids are going to school in the dark," Rodríguez Ferrante said. "Keep in mind that we used the actual start time listed for each school, and a lot of schools offer breakfast or other things before school, so the kids could be getting there even earlier."

Why the 2 Billion Estimate May Be Too Low

Although the researchers used detailed school information to calculate changes in 14 states, their nationwide estimate required broader assumptions. To project what would happen if the entire United States adopted permanent daylight saving time, they assumed students would generally be leaving for school at around 8 a.m.

Because many children begin traveling earlier, the team believes the projected increase of approximately 2 billion dark commutes may substantially underestimate the actual impact.

"For the estimation, we assumed students would be leaving home around 8 a.m.," Rodríguez Ferrante said. "That's pretty late, so our calculation is likely an underestimation of the real number."

The findings also raise questions about efforts to improve teenagers' sleep by delaying high school start times. Adolescents typically have biological clocks that shift later than those of younger children and adults, making later school schedules beneficial. The researchers argue that permanently moving clocks forward could undermine some of those gains by making morning sunlight less accessible.

One possible solution would be to start school later to compensate for the darker mornings. However, de la Iglesia argues that such a change could have ripple effects throughout daily life, potentially requiring families and workplaces to adjust their schedules as well.

"I've heard the argument, 'If we're in permanent DST, we can just delay the school start time to address these issues,'" de la Iglesia said. "Well, if we do that, you will end up going to work later. And everything is going to get delayed. You will get out of work an hour later, and you will miss the opportunity to enjoy your evening light. And essentially, we're just going to be realigning everybody to solar time. That, by definition, is Standard Time."

The researchers' findings highlight a central tradeoff in the debate over permanent daylight saving time. While eliminating seasonal clock changes would provide more evening sunlight during winter, the additional daylight would come at the expense of morning light, potentially affecting children's safety, sleep, and daily routines.

Additional study authors include high school student Daniel Zhang and University of Washington biology undergraduates Nirekh Dasika, Alicia Nam, Jessie Lu, Navneet Tumber, Elena Kully-Rivera, Viridian Klei, and Micaela E. Romero.

Venus Express had to survive harsh radiation at Venus, but it persevered for nine years.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 8, 2005, Europe launched its first mission to Venus. The spacecraft was called Venus Express.

Venus is a hothouse planet, one where the atmospheric pressure can easily crush an unprotected spacecraft. Even from orbit, Venus Express had to survive harsh radiation. But the spacecraft lasted for more than nine years.

During that time, Venus Express saw a weird vortex swirling around Venus's south pole. It also saw possible signs of active volcanoes. Venus Express also discovered that the planet generates its own auroras. These auroras happen when particles from the sun hit charged particles in the atmosphere.

Late in the Venus Express mission, controllers told the spacecraft to dip down into Venus's clouds — even though the spacecraft wasn't designed to do this. It performed well, but eventually it stopped listening to commands. The spacecraft burned up in the atmosphere in January 2015.

Venus Express established ESA as the third world organization to successfully send a probe to study Venus, following the United States and Soviet Union. (Japan's JAXA became the fourth five years later.)

"By studying Venus, scientists learn how Earth-like planets change over time," reads a summary of the planet's exploration prepared by The Planetary Society. "Orbital studies [like Venus Express] hint that Venus may have hosted habitable oceans before becoming inhospitable."

"By studying Venus, we can learn how Earth-like planets evolve and what shapes planets throughout the galaxy into temperate, lush worlds instead of sweltering hothouses. Venus also helps scientists model Earth’s climate, and may serve as a cautionary tale on how dramatically a planet’s climate can change," wrote the Society.

ESA returned to Venus in 2018 when BepiColombo, its joint mission with JAXA, used the planet's gravity to redirect its path toward the planet Mercury.

Fisher will star in the new musical after leading roles in 'Moulin Rouge!' 'Hadestown' and more.

Jordan Fisher will star as “The Kid” in the Broadway stage adaptation of Purple Rain.

A Broadway veteran, known for his starring roles in Moulin Rouge!, Hadestown and Dear Evan Hansen, Fisher takes on the role played by Prince in the 1984 film. The musical is set to start previews March 12, 2027 at the Majestic Theatre, ahead of an April 12 opening.

An alternate performer to be announced will play the role of “The Kid” on Tuesday evenings and Wednesday matinees. Additional casting will be announced at a later date.

The musical, based on the film, features music by Prince, including “When Doves Cry,” “I Would Die 4 U,” “Take Me with You” and “Purple Rain.” The musical follows a young performer known as “The Kid,” who tries to lead his band to fame, while dealing with his own turbulent past, a rival singer and a developing romantic interest.

In addition to his Broadway credits, which also include Laurens/Philip in Hamilton and Anthony in the most recent revival of Sweeney Todd, Fisher has starred on screen in Netflix’s Hello, Goodbye, and Everything in Between, To All the Boys: P.S. I Still Love You, Work It, Rent: Live!, Grease: Live!, and Disney/Pixar’s Turning Red.

“We know that Jordan Fisher is an extraordinary talent, but what’s been thrilling about watching him inhabit ‘The Kid’ is discovering the fire beneath the surface: the swagger, vulnerability and restless creative spirit we recognize in Prince,” said director Saheem Ali. “Jordan brings all of that to the role, along with an infectious generosity that makes everyone around him better. He’s finding something raw, surprising, and deeply human in this iconic character, and I can’t wait for Broadway audiences to experience it.”

The musical comes to Broadway after a world premiere at the State Theater in Minneapolis in fall 2025. The show has since revamped its creative team, with Ali (Buena Vista Social Club) now directing the musical and a new book by Peter Duchan (Dogfight). Choreographer Ebony Williams remains (Sneakerella; additional choreography for the Renaissance World Tour). Kris Kollins, a D.C-based singer songwriter, played the role of the Kid in Minnesota.

Bobby Z and Morris Hayes, both of whom worked with Prince, are music advisers on the production. Orin Wolf, producer of Buena Vista Social Club, is lead producing.

#739. Five-inch-long beetle larvae are quietly destroying blueberry roots

North Carolina's blueberry growers are facing an emerging threat from a destructive beetle whose larvae feed underground, damaging plant roots and potentially killing blueberry bushes. Scientists have now identified the insect responsible, providing an important first step toward protecting crops from the pest.

A research team at North Carolina State University has confirmed that the culprit is Prionus imbricornus, a species of longhorn beetle distinguished by its long antennae. These wood-boring insects are becoming a growing concern for blueberry producers in the state.

Female beetles generally deposit their eggs in soil near the roots of hardwood trees. After hatching, the larvae feed on the roots, sometimes destroying enough tissue to kill the tree. The larvae can reach an impressive five inches in length, while the adult beetles do not feed.

A Decade-Old Mystery Beneath Blueberry Fields

North Carolina is the first state to document P. imbricornus feeding on blueberry bushes. However, signs of a similar problem have existed for years. Reports of unidentified Prionus larvae damaging blueberry roots date back to 2010, but researchers had struggled to determine which species was responsible.

Part of the challenge was the insects' underground habitat. Because the larvae remain near plant roots, they are difficult to locate and study. Making matters more complicated, larvae from different longhorn beetle species often look remarkably similar, making visual identification unreliable.

According to Kenneth Geisert, a graduate student in NC State's College of Agriculture and Life Sciences and lead author of the study, this uncertainty has made it difficult to develop appropriate pest control strategies.

"Before now, researchers often just assumed the species of Prionus on their commodities based on adult identification," Geisert said. "If that guess was incorrect, it could mean using a treatment strategy that did not line up with the problem and incorrectly associating species and their hosts. For instance, while P. imbricornus attacks roots, another type of longhorn beetle might attack the trunk of a tree, or dead branches. Without knowing which species of beetle you're dealing with and their ecology, incorrect management can cause adverse effects on non-target insects."

To identify the insects, the research team conducted fieldwork at six blueberry farms in North Carolina's Pender, Sampson, Bladen, and New Hanover counties.

The scientists installed black panel traps containing sex pheromones, chemical signals that attract adult beetles. After collecting the insects, they used a DNA identification technique known as genetic barcoding to determine the identity of larvae found in the fields.

This method examines short, standardized sections of DNA and compares them with reference sequences from known species. By matching genetic material from the unidentified larvae with DNA from adult Prionus beetles, the researchers could determine which species was present.

The analysis produced a 98 to 99 percent match with P. imbricornus, confirming the identity of the beetle responsible for the root damage.

A Growing Threat With No Approved Insecticides

Although identifying the pest represents an important breakthrough, it also highlights a serious challenge for blueberry growers.

Lorena Lopez, an assistant extension professor in NC State's Department of Entomology and Plant Pathology and a co-author of the study, explained that the discovery brings both encouraging and troubling news.

"On one hand, it's very important that we know which species we're dealing with," she said. "On the other, North Carolina was the first state to ever report Prionus infestation in blueberries, and there are no insecticides currently labeled against this pest in blueberries."

To help address this problem, Lopez has begun testing insecticides to determine which treatments might effectively control the beetles.

A major focus is finding the best time to apply treatments. By coordinating insecticide applications with the beetles' reproductive cycles, researchers hope to disrupt larval development before the insects can inflict extensive damage on blueberry roots.

If successful, this approach could give farmers a much-needed way to protect their crops against an emerging pest that has remained difficult to identify and manage for more than a decade.

The findings appear in the Journal of Integrated Pest Management in a paper titled "Prionus imbricornis (Coleoptera: Cerambycidae), an emerging pest in North Carolina blueberries." Gareth Powell, an assistant professor at NC State and director of the NCSU Insect Museum, also contributed to the research.

"Starlog" was one of the greatest sci-fi and fantasy magazines ever, and after a 17-year absence, it's being resurrected.

The legendary sci-fi mag went dark back in 2009 as part of the wave of popular publications folding due to years of declining readership and subscriptions. But as of Nov. 13, this geek favorite periodical returns as an annual print edition, and it's available for pre-order now.

It’s another indication of digital fatigue in the world, and fans of a certain age will recall the pleasure of poring over each colorful issue packed with in-depth interviews, behind-the-scenes photos, TV guides, classic movie retrospectives, book reviews, con news, and VFX features.

"Starlog" launched in 1976, in the pre-"Star Wars" days, under the leadership of editor-in-chief Kerry O’Quinn. It first arrived with artist Jack Thurston's beautiful painted "Star Trek" cover, featuring William Shatner as Captain James T. Kirk and Leonard Nimoy’s Spock, set against the U.S.S. Enterprise near a shimmering black hole.

The magazine continued to inform the science fiction community about upcoming sci-fi TV shows and blockbuster Hollywood films for over three decades; I fondly recall reading each informative and entertaining monthly issue cover-to-cover.

Just in time to honor its 50th anniversary this year, "Starlog" blasts back into the sci-fi universe with Issue #375 showcasing cover artwork created by Armenian artist Gabriel Yeganyan. Its geek culture legacy, covering iconic franchises like "Star Wars," "Star Trek," and "Alien," will now live on thanks to Fangoria Holdings and io9 co-founder Annalee Newitz, editor-in-chief.

"During its original 33-year run, 'Starlog' documented science fiction as it evolved across film, television, books, technology, and culture," said 'Fangoria's Tara Ansley.

"Fifty years after the magazine first launched, the line between science fiction and the real world has become increasingly difficult to separate. That makes this an especially interesting time to bring 'Starlog' back. Technology may change, but the most compelling questions have always been about people: how we live, what we create, and what kind of future we want to build."

"Starlog" reloads for its first annual edition after a long hiatus on Nov. 13. You can pre-order the first issue (Issue 375 in continuity) on the Starlog website.

Jeff Spry is an award-winning screenwriter and veteran freelance journalist covering TV, movies, video games, books, and comics. His work has appeared at SYFY Wire, Inverse, Collider, Bleeding Cool and elsewhere. Jeff lives in beautiful Bend, Oregon amid the ponderosa pines, classic muscle cars, a crypt of collector horror comics, and two loyal English Setters.

#737. Skydance Earnings: Wall Street Is Skeptical So Far

Analysts react to the first post-Warner Bros. acquisition quarterly results of David Ellison’s Hollywood giant, with one wondering how this merger can succeed when "so many other major media deals have failed."

Skydance’s first quarterly earnings report after the mega-acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery (WBD) is in. And Wall Street’s take on the results and especially the outlook for David Ellison’s Hollywood giant is … still under review.

The results, posted after the market close on Monday, came a year after Paramount’s first financials under the leadership of Ellison. On the earnings call, the Skydance chairman and CEO expressed bullishness on the creative potential of AI. And he addressed the surprise leadership change at DC Studios, with Marvel alum Jeremy Latcham replacing James Gunn and Peter Safran.

Skydance shares were down more than 2 percent to $8.50 in pre-market trading. So, what did Wall Street analysts take away from the entertainment conglomerate’s first financial and strategic update since the WBD deal close? The Hollywood Reporter is compiling key commentary and thoughts below.

Analyst: Laurent Yoon, BernsteinStock rating and price target: underperform, $6Takeaways: “Trailer Looks Good… Waiting for the Movie” was the title of Yoon’s report following the latest results. “The third quarter was more of a prologue than Chapter 1 of Skydance’s journey following the WBD acquisition,” he wrote. “Pro forma financials with WBD won’t be available until sometime before the fourth-quarter print, leaving us on the edge of how this story could unfold. There are more questions than answers, but we come out net positive.”One of the key questions, or developing stories, if you will, is the studio. “Legacy WBD seems likely to be a drag near-term, particularly in the fourth quarter,” the analyst concluded. “Studio performance has underperformed, with management flagging an up to a around $200 million fourth-quarter profit shortfall from WBD theatrical performance. WBD’s larger linear exposure also remains a likely drag, though it represents meaningful opportunity for operating expense synergies.”So, what will investors need to get more bullish? “The raw ingredients are there to build something better than the individual parts. And we wait for Chapter 1.”

Analyst: Michael Morris, Guggenheim SecuritiesStock rating and price target: neutral, no price targetTakeaways: “Skydance’s first report since closing the WBD acquisition showed continued progress at legacy Paramount and limited incremental detail on the combined company,” Morris wrote in his report entitled “Awaiting Takeoff.” He currently doesn’t have a price target on the stock, citing “the lack of historical pro forma disclosure and no third-quarter operating results for legacy Warner Bros. Discovery.” His rating “balances potential upside from synergies and streaming scale against execution risk and the combined company’s higher leverage.”The analyst also outlined what he is looking for now. “We believe the market has heard the strategy and needs evidence of progress in three areas: 1) a content slate that bolsters confidence in consumer demand for core franchises, 2) the net financial impact of combining HBO Max and Paramount+, beginning with the early 2027 bundle, and 3) management of the declining but cash-generative linear business.”Morris highlighted that Warner Bros. is a work in progress, highlighting that management called the studio on track “with the exception of the near-term film slate.” Noting an up to $200 million fourth-quarter profit impact from films already released this quarter and those still to come, the analyst described the DC Studios leadership change as “the first structural response.” And he added: “The 2027 Warner Bros. slate (Godzilla x Kong: Supernova, Man of Tomorrow, A Minecraft Movie Squared, the Ocean’s Eleven prequel, The Lord of the Rings: The Hunt for Gollum) is where Paramount’s greenlight and marketing discipline should show up.”

Analyst: Doug Creutz, TD CowenStock rating and price target: hold, $8Takeaways: Because the WBD deal closed after the end of the third quarter, the latest results reflect “Paramount Skydance standalone results,” the analyst emphasized, summarizing: “Paramount’s standalone third-quarter adjusted EBITDA of $1.0 billion beat our $947 million estimate on stronger DTC and Studios profit, though revenue of $7.03 billion was below our estimate of $7.13 billion.”The TD Cowen expert also noted that management reiterated its target of at least $6 billion in deal synergies within three years and “gave the first breakdown by category,” namely at least $2.2 billion from corporate overhead, real estate, and facilities, $1.4 billion from technology, $1.4 billion from procurement and vendor management, and $1.0 billion from marketing. About 30 percent of those synergies should be in place by the end of 2027.All that said, Creutz continues to have doubts, sharing this investment thesis: “The risks (leverage, integration) of the combination with WBD are high; we remain skeptical that Skydance management will be able to create value from this deal when so many other major media deals have failed.”

Analyst: Robert Fishman, MoffettNathansonStock rating and price target: neutral, $7Takeaways: “Ghosts of the Past, Present and Future” was the title of Fishman’s report, a timely Charles Dickens reference just before Skydance releases Ebenezer, starring Johnny Depp. “After last night’s earnings report, we get a first glimpse of how Skydance views its trajectory in relation to some … questions [we have previously outlined] but still lots of questions remain.”Among them is whether the merged company can balance cost cuts and growth investments. Looking at the areas that Skydance said it would find efficiencies in, the MoffettNathanson analyst offered: “In theory, savings in these areas should get the company to its synergy targets without dipping into its $30 billion-plus of content spending, allowing it to pay down debt without sacrificing growth. However, as we’ve seen with other media M&A, it is a lot harder to see these cost savings translate into real upside to EBITDA and cash flows, likely forcing the company to limit its content spend growth in the future.”And he highlighted a need for investor and analyst patience for a closer look under the hood until Skydance discloses pro forma financials for its business plus WBD early in 2027. For now, he left most of his estimates unchanged.

#736. Head Marge Liiske on Tallinn Market, One of Northern Europe’s Largest Industry-Training Confabs, Now Turning 25

Industry @ Tallinn & Baltic Event, one of Northern Europe’s largest training and industry confabs, is celebrating its 25th anniversary with a packed program where the Baltics stand at its core, as part of Tallinn’s Black Night Film Festival’s own milestone 30th edition.

A record 900 accredited professionals from 54 countries – including around 100 sales agents, distributors and festival programmers – have signed up for the event which will showcase 71 projects (44 films and 21 series) and focus on audience design, sales and distribution through 100-plus panels, on top of industry training via the Discovery Campus strand. Related Stories Lula’s Election Win: How Fan Accounts for Taylor Swift, Billie Eilish and More Helped Him to a Historic Victory and Defeat for Trump Bill Maher Fires Back at Trump by Comparing Him to Taylor Swift

Speaking with Variety as the 12-day industry event just kickstarted, Marge Liiske, the industry boss of it all, drilled down on the program’s highlights, its past achievements and prospects for the gigantic industry showcase which has played a key role in developing the audiovisual industry in Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania.

Industry @ Tallinn & Baltic Event (ITBE) Turns 25. Could you take us through the changes that you’ve experienced since you joined the confab, and the next steps ahead?

Marge Liiske: I joined in 2013 to run the Baltic Event Co-Production Market, after seven years at the Estonian Film Foundation. In 2016 I took over the whole platform. My first priority was to merge our two strands, Industry@Tallinn and Baltic Event, so that guests would have a single entry point, program and set of services. Today that umbrella is a brand of its own, and it works seamlessly. Another boost came gradually: PÖFF [the Black Nights Film Festival] had received its A-category status in 2014, and over the following years it brought more press, sales agents and producers to Tallinn.

Since then, we have grown by adding new layers rather than by enlarging one market. Series arrived in 2017 with the world premiere of “Babylon Berlin” and have grown into TV Beats, with its conference program, co-financing market, screenings and showcases. Our talent programs grew strand by strand and are now united under the Discovery Campus, with seven programs. The short film industry program followed in 2021, children’s and youth film got its own industry days in 2023 and its own category in the Co-Production Market a year later.

Next, we want to do more for distributors and exhibitors, an area we would like to strengthen. Documentary is another: this year at least 15 documentary projects in development asked to join the co-production market, and we regularly get requests for documentary works in progress. The Discovery Campus also has exciting plans for 2027, which we will announce early next year. And we have some new ideas for the Co-Production Market, which we will reveal in spring 2027.

What are your main focal points this year?

Liiske: Each year we choose a focus. Last year it was financing; this year it is audience design, sales and distribution, both theatrical and digital. We want to give producers very hands-on tools: how to design an audience strategy from the start, when a sales agent should come on board, and how a film can reach viewers in cinemas and online. Friday Nov. 20 is dedicated entirely to sales, distribution and audience design, so producers can spend a full day with the people who will bring their films to audiences. Then our Focus Countries this year are the Baltics, with 310 Baltic professionals, 81 films, 21 projects, 19 talents in Discovery Campus. We are so excited to present them in different screenings and sessions, plus a showcase on Nov. 19. We also have a Spotlight on Basque Audiovisual with a delegation of 10 professionals, nine films and three projects.

What structural changes have you made? All 16 works in progress are on Nov. 19, and there seem to be new venues…

Liiske: We have made the schedule more concentrated. The Script Pool and Co-Production Market projects now all present on the afternoon of Wednesday Nov. 18. The works in progress follow in the morning and early afternoon of Thursday Nov. 19, leaving the teams the rest of Thursday and all of Friday to talk, mingle and build partnerships before the closing ceremony [Nov. 20]. The Discovery Campus now has its own Discovery Hub at the Tallink Spa & Conference Hotel, giving talents a home base where they can spend more time with each other.

Baltic films are thriving internationally and new studios are being built. What challenges still lie ahead for the Baltic audiovisual industry?

Liiske: The biggest challenge is turning visibility into continuity in our small markets. A “Flow,” a “Smoke Sauna Sisterhood” or a “Toxic” creates a moment, but producers need the next film, and companies need to survive between projects. Our national funds alone cannot finance ambitious work, so international partners are a necessity.

The new studios are an important step, and we present the new IDA Hub film complex at the event this year. But infrastructure also needs projects and skilled crews to fill it, and those take time to build. Keeping talent in the region while giving them international careers is part of that. And our national films need to keep finding their audiences, both at home and at festivals.

We are also very proud to showcase two Estonian startups: the IRIS casting database and Mureel platform, building sustainability and ESG compliance infrastructure for the European audiovisual industry.

What trends do you see in co-productions with the Baltics?

Liiske: Producers bring in partners earlier, and those partners come from further away: no longer only neighbours, but France, Italy, Poland and beyond. Our Co-Production Market brings together 15 projects from 10 countries this year, and eight of them are by debut directors, which shows how early international co-production now begins in a filmmaker’s career.

We also see growing interest in the Baltics from established production countries. That’s why this year we organise meetings between French and Baltic producers, and a meet-up for emerging Finnish and Estonian producers. Children’s and youth films and genre projects are other clear trends: children’s and youth projects have their own category in the market, genre projects have the European Genre Forum, and the quality keeps rising.

TV Beats continues to grow. Could you comment on this year’s program, including the screenings opening with the latest season of ‘Babylon Berlin’?

Liiske: “Babylon Berlin is a home-coming for us. The series had its world premiere at PÖFF in 2017, the year we brought series into our industry program, so it is a pleasure to present the new season here among the seven TV Beats screenings.

TV Beats has grown step by step: the forum, then the co-financing market, the screenings, and last year Coming Soon from the Baltics. This year, for the first time, we opened international calls for both the Screenings and Coming Soon.

This year’s forum looks at how creators can shape new ideas into scripts and attract international attention. It also looks both east and west, with the Finnish-Japanese journey of “Blood & Sweat” and “Dear X” from Korea. A session on the showrunner model explores how history and politics shape it across European traditions, and the European Writers Club invites writers to create stories together. And with seven series screenings, there is always something to binge between meetings.

Training of Baltic -and international- professionals-is at the core of PÖFF and ITBE. What are the Discovery Campus highlights? Could you also briefly discuss the Tallinn Industry Academy and Breaking into the Industry strands?

Liiske: Discovery Campus opens with Sir Christopher Hampton, Academy Award winner for “Dangerous Liaisons” and “The Father,” speaking about adaptation. Craft sessions follow with cinematographers Julio Macat (“Home Alone”), Roberto Schaefer (“Finding Neverland,””The Kite Runner”), David Stump (“X-Men,””Deep Blue Sea”), Dan Laustsen (“Frankenstein”) and Michael Bauman, composer Martin Phipps, production designer Inbal Weinberg (“The Room Next Door,” “Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri”), and casting directors Yngvild Haga (“Sentimental Value”), Pauline Hansson and Nina Haun (“Triangle of Sadness”), among others.

Bringing the Tallinn Industry Academy and Breaking into the Industry into the Discovery Campus this year gives emerging talents and future filmmakers more chances to meet, exchange ideas and build their networks. The Campus also has its own dedicated space for the first time, the Discovery Hub.

How are issues related to the younger generation, integrated into the Just Film Industry Days program for children and youth?

Liiske: Children and young people are tomorrow’s audience, so understanding how they think and what they value matters to the whole industry. That’s why we don’t keep children’s and youth film in a separate bubble. Just Film Industry Days, now in their fourth edition, run alongside the rest of the market, and the professionals mix.

This year, film literacy is at the heart of the programme. We look at how young viewers discover films as their access to social media changes, why audiovisual literacy deserves our attention, and what research reveals about the visual language of children’s films.

Children’s and youth projects also take part in both the Co-Production Market and the Works in Progress, so they get the same attention from sales agents and distributors as any other film.

What’s your take on current AI trends, and how is the topic explored at ITBE?

Liiske: What interests me most is not the tools themselves, but how they change who gets to tell stories, and how. AI can open doors for small teams and smaller countries like ours, but only if the human vision stays in charge. Otherwise it does not make any sense.

AI was very present in our program in recent years. We ran AI ateliers and approached AI not as something to fear, but as something we can shape. This year we have consciously taken some distance: AI has entered our lives so deeply that it is almost impossible to talk about it as a separate entity.

That doesn’t mean we’ve stopped working on it. Throughout the year, we have run Mastering AI for European Film Professionals, a five-module training program supported by Creative Europe MEDIA. In November, we keep one focused session, which asks whether AI can serve hand-crafted, cross-cultural storytelling with a human storyteller in charge. Edmond Yang, Gold winner at Project Odyssey and Gullhaien and a creative partner of Runway and Luma, will open up the workflows behind his animation and hybrid films.

How do you deal with higher costs and inflation in Estonia? Who are your main backers and key partners?

Liiske: We have had to become more efficient, but also reduce the number of free services for our guests, which of course is sad, but it’s life; Estonia has become quite an expensive country. We are also more selective about whose expenses we cover: we invest in guests who actively engage with our projects.

Our main backers are Creative Europe MEDIA, which has just renewed its support for our market, the Estonian Ministry of Culture, the Cultural Endowment of Estonia, the Estonian Film Institute, the City of Tallinn and the Estonian Business and Innovation Agency, as well as neighbouring film institutes. Our key partners include Eurimages, which gives the Co-Production Development Award, and the Council of Europe, with its €50,000 ($56,000) Series Co-Production Development Award at TV Beats. We are also very grateful to long-standing partners such as Studio Beep, ATM Virtual and many others. This year we counted 72 partners, and without exaggeration, every one of them is valuable to us.
