#735. Scientists accidentally solve a chemistry mystery that lasted 60 years

A chemistry challenge that had frustrated researchers for more than 60 years has finally been overcome. Scientists at the University of Würzburg in Germany have discovered a way to produce and isolate oxoboranes, a group of unusual molecules that were long considered too unstable to study under ordinary laboratory conditions.

The breakthrough, published in Nature Chemistry, was led by Professor Holger Braunschweig and his team, with computational support from researchers led by Professor Ashwini K. Phukan at Tezpur University in India. Their findings reveal a surprisingly straightforward way to create these elusive compounds, potentially opening new possibilities for molecular chemistry.

Boron is an element that rarely forms triple bonds, a type of chemical connection in which two atoms share three pairs of electrons. For more than 15 years, Braunschweig has focused on overcoming this limitation and creating molecules containing unusual bonds involving boron.

His laboratory has already achieved several important milestones. In 2012, the team reported the first molecule containing a triple bond between two boron atoms. Another breakthrough followed in 2025, when the researchers produced the first neutral molecule featuring a triple bond between boron and carbon.

One major challenge remained among the elements in the first row of the periodic table's p-block. Researchers had yet to isolate stable organic oxoboranes, molecules characterized by a triple bond between boron and oxygen.

Chemists around the world had been pursuing these compounds since at least the early 1960s. Over the decades, scientists working in both organic and inorganic chemistry had managed to detect and trap oxoboranes under extreme conditions. Other experiments provided indirect evidence of their existence, and researchers succeeded in creating several related derivatives. However, obtaining stable examples that could be isolated and examined remained an unsolved problem.

An Unexpected Reaction Produces Elusive Molecules

The long-awaited breakthrough emerged from experiments that initially appeared to be heading in a different direction.

Two doctoral students at the University of Würzburg, Lukas Lubczyk and Christian Markl, were independently investigating reactions between a compound known as a diboracumulene and various ketones, which are commonly used chemicals in organic synthesis.

Both researchers noticed something unusual. Instead of producing only the outcomes they might have expected, the reactions generated distinctive orange or yellow solids.

"The discovery was a pleasant surprise. I never thought the diboracumulene would react the way it did, let alone with multiple different, simple substrates. And when Christian came to me with his compound, I knew we were onto something," says Lukas Lubczyk.

What made the results particularly remarkable was that oxoboranes emerged as the main products of these reactions, even though several other chemical outcomes had appeared more likely. After decades of unsuccessful efforts to isolate such molecules, the researchers had found that they could form unexpectedly from reactions involving relatively simple starting materials.

Braunschweig described just how surprising the discovery was to scientists familiar with the long-standing challenge.

"Nearly everybody in the field had given up on oxoboranes, as they were thought to be just too unstable to be isolated. So we were stunned to see them spontaneously form in these reactions and stick around long enough that we could study them," says Holger Braunschweig.

Using their newly discovered method, the scientists successfully prepared three different oxoboranes. The fact that the approach worked with multiple compounds suggests that it could provide access to a much wider range of these previously difficult to isolate molecules.

The team is now investigating how broadly the technique can be applied. Beyond producing additional oxoboranes, the researchers hope to determine whether similar strategies could help them create other elusive compounds involving elements throughout the periodic table.

The discovery not only resolves a problem that challenged chemists for more than six decades but also demonstrates how unexpected chemical reactions can reveal possibilities that researchers once considered beyond reach.

International Research Collaboration and Funding

The findings were published through a collaboration between the Würzburg research team and the group led by Professor Ashwini K. Phukan at Tezpur University (India), whose computational research helped support the work.

Funding was provided by the German Research Foundation (DFG), the German Academic Exchange Service (DAAD), and the Department of Science & Technology (DST) of India.

"Our tiny ground station shouted at an ESA spacecraft, and was heard."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A satellite went knee-deep in the dead, after a voice command from the ground activated the Doom video game in space.

Playing a first-person shooter from 1993 was obviously not in the design plan for the PRETTY cubesat, which is run by a consortium including the European Space Agency (ESA). But the pioneering voice command opens up new worlds for satellite work, the team says.

"Someone in distress at sea or in a remote area could transmit 'mayday' or "help" on a radio," stated Estonia's Tanagra Space, which supplied the software for the feat. The hope is one day, a satellite could use transcription and AI to alert rescue services for assisting folks in remote zones.

The call to play Doom, thankfully, had no other urgency than curiosity — and teamwork, fueled by pizza. OPS-SAT Space Lab managed the experiment on behalf of ESA. Radio amateurs then made six unsuccessful attempts during passes over Poland and Norway, between April and July. The seventh finally reached success under the Oslo Group of the Norwegian Radio Relay League.

"We are radio amateurs, with the emphasis on amateurs. Satellite work was not something our club did, and we had no budget for it," representative Eskil Hadland, call sign LB6AJ, said in the Tangara statement. "So we borrowed a line wrongly credited to Pippi Longstocking: 'I have never tried that before, so I should definitely be able to do that.'"

The Norwegians spent 59 days and about 7200 NOK or $775 (pizza included) to reach PRETTY, helping make changes to the satellite software to pick up a voice. For example, a raw recording of an attempt on July 3, retransmitted to Earth, showed the spoken words to space were unrecognizable. Further work revealed the satellite's receiver channel was too wide to pick up the voice signal, leading to a fix to narrow the channel.

The historic voice command on July 27— in part, "PRETTY play Doom Doom Doom"— came from a rooftop in Oslo, and was spoken at night by Jon Bergli Heier (LB9BJ). PRETTY picked up the transmission, transcribed the command using on-board voice recognition, and then — just like a typical evening gamer—opened up Doom for a play session.

This was no multiplayer gaming situation, but the satellite did create a report of its demon-slaying skills — and its ability to interpret the command. For example, PRETTY generated a "postcard" including a frame of the gameplay, a transcription, and signal diagnostics. The satellite also transmitted its recording of Hadland's command.

As anybody who uses voice-recognition software knows, there are challenges in transcriptions: nobody speaks in exactly the same way, and aspects such as accent or background noise can lead to misinterpretations. The satellite also had to contend with Doppler shift, and with an antenna not designed to relay voices to space.

But the transmission clearly worked, powered by open-source tools including GNU Radio (which handled the signal processing) and Sherpa-ONNX (speech recognition).

The hope is that future spacecraft could one day adapt this approach to radio frequencies for other ideas outside of spoken words. For example, perhaps deep-space radio signals could be detected via satellite, with an AI on board sending the most relevant data to operators after analyzing the work.

For now, however, the Norwegian radio operators are basking in the success: "Our tiny ground station shouted at an ESA spacecraft, and was heard," Hadland said.

Elizabeth Howell (she/her), Ph.D., was a staff writer in the spaceflight channel between 2022 and 2024 specializing in Canadian space news. She was contributing writer for Space.com for 10 years from 2012 to 2024. Elizabeth's reporting includes multiple exclusives with the White House, leading world coverage about a lost-and-found space tomato on the International Space Station, witnessing five human spaceflight launches on two continents, flying parabolic, working inside a spacesuit, and participating in a simulated Mars mission. #733. Webby Awards Launches IMDB-Like Credits Platform to Provide Verified Recognition for Creators Amid AI Growth (Exclusive)

The long-running initiative celebrating the best of the internet will allow winners, nominees and other honored individuals to claim their work, with Shonda Rhimes and Adam Scott among the founding members.

After celebrating its 30th anniversary earlier this year, the Webby Awards is making it easier for winners, nominees and other honored individuals to make sure they’re properly credited for their work.

The IMDB-like Global Webby Credits Registry allows creators, developers, producers, writers and actors to claim verified profiles documenting their contributions. Though the Webbys have long included these names at the bottom of project pages, the profiles bring together a career’s worth of recognized work regardless of whether the people behind these projects move between different companies. Related Stories Movies Ridley Scott Will Miss Academy's Governors Awards, Accept Honorary Oscar Remotely (Exclusive) Movies 'You Can See Everything' Sweeps Critics Choice Documentary Awards

“The people behind great creative work on the internet have never been harder to find, and they’ve never mattered more,” Webby Group executive director Jesse Feister said in a statement. “The Global Webby Credits Registry puts 30 years of Webby recognition in the hands of the more than 150,000 individuals who earned it, and the thousands who will earn it in the years ahead, giving them verified credentials to build reputation in the AI era.”

As AI becomes a bigger tool in both the discovery of information and the generation of creative work, the Webbys argue these verified credits provide a better way to ensure people are recognized for what they’ve made.

“AI is changing how we discover information, including information about people and their work. Search results are increasingly summarized by AI, and as the technology evolves, we expect more of the ways people discover and evaluate creative professionals to be mediated by AI tools,” Feister tells The Hollywood Reporter. “That makes credible, independent records of people’s work more important than ever. A credit on an award-winning project is a meaningful professional credential, but only if that credit is documented somewhere it can be found and trusted. And as AI makes it easier than ever to produce creative work, having a credible record of what you’ve actually contributed to becomes more important, too.”

A number of Webby-recognized individuals, like Shonda Rhimes and Adam Scott, have already published their own verified profiles as founding members. The launch of the Webbys’ credits platform is also being supported by companies that have won Webbys in the past, including PBS, iHeartMedia and R/GA.

“Behind every great PBS digital experience is a team of talented people bringing our mission to life,” PBS’ vice president, multiplatform marketing and content, Amy Wigler, said in a statement. “The Webby Credits Registry gives those individuals recognition that stays with them throughout their careers. We’re excited to help celebrate their contributions and make their work more visible.”

To claim a profile, eligible individuals can search the Webby Credits database for projects they contributed to, claim the credits associated with their work, verify their identity through LinkedIn and publish their profile. As new work is recognized, the people behind those projects can claim their credits as well.

#732. Scientists discover that a clogged filter could revolutionize oil refining

Researchers have developed a surprisingly simple way to separate crude oil without heating it, potentially transforming one of the world's most energy-intensive industrial processes. The breakthrough uses an inexpensive membrane that could significantly reduce the energy required for oil refining while lowering operating costs and carbon emissions.

The international research effort was led by Professor Dong-Yeun Koh at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, known as KAIST, in collaboration with Professor Ryan Lively's research group at Georgia Tech. KAIST(President Kwang Hyung Lee) announced that the team had successfully demonstrated a membrane capable of separating crude oil at room temperature. The findings were published in Nature, one of the world's leading scientific journals.

Crude oil is essential for far more than gasoline and other transportation fuels. It also supplies the raw materials used to manufacture plastics, packaging, clothing, and numerous everyday products. Because refining costs affect the prices of these materials, making the process more efficient could have widespread economic and environmental benefits.

Why Traditional Crude Oil Refining Requires So Much Energy

For more than a century, oil refineries have relied heavily on distillation to separate crude oil into useful components. The process involves heating oil to temperatures above 350 °C, turning portions of it into vapor, and then cooling those vapors to collect different fractions.

This approach requires an enormous amount of energy. Worldwide, crude oil distillation consumes approximately 1,100 terawatt-hours (TWh) annually. That is comparable to the combined yearly electricity production of roughly 130 continuously operating nuclear power plants, each with a capacity of about one gigawatt.

The massive energy demand makes distillation a major contributor to both fuel consumption and greenhouse gas emissions within the refining industry. Meanwhile, growing economic pressures across global petrochemical markets have increased interest in technologies that can separate oil more efficiently.

Membranes have emerged as a promising alternative because they can separate substances without requiring the extreme temperatures used in conventional distillation. However, previous designs have faced significant obstacles.

Traditionally, researchers have assumed that effective molecular separation requires a membrane covered with an extremely thin, specialized coating. Although these coatings can provide the necessary precision, they are expensive to produce and can develop defects when manufactured on a large scale. These limitations have made widespread industrial adoption difficult.

A Surprising Discovery Turns Clogged Filters Into an Advantage

The KAIST and Georgia Tech researchers approached the problem differently. Rather than adding a complicated coating, they used a bare membrane made from porous polyacrylonitrile (PAN), an inexpensive, chemically stable polymer already commonly used as a supporting material in industrial filtration systems.

What happened when crude oil passed through the membrane was unexpected.

As the oil flowed through its pores, heavier hydrocarbon molecules accumulated along the inner walls. This buildup gradually reduced the size of the openings, producing extremely narrow channels measuring less than 2 nanometers across.

In effect, the crude oil helped create the microscopic pathways needed to separate its own components.

These naturally formed channels allowed lighter oil fractions, including naphtha, gasoline, and kerosene, to pass through quickly while preventing heavier substances from traveling through the membrane as easily.

The discovery was especially surprising because the buildup of material inside membrane pores, known as fouling, is normally considered a serious problem. Fouling typically reduces filtration performance and requires cleaning or replacement. In this case, however, the same phenomenon made the membrane highly effective at separating different molecules.

The results were impressive. The uncoated PAN membrane achieved crude oil permeation rates approximately 23 times higher than those reported for previous leading crude oil separation membranes. It also continued operating with stable performance for 28 consecutive days.

Professor Ryan Lively (Georgia Tech) commented: "One of the key challenges facing membrane systems for crude oil separation was the low productivities of the membrane units -- the PAN membranes with their surprising separation mechanism -- dramatically increase the productivity of the membrane unit, to the point where industry should seriously consider adopting the technology."

New Membrane Could Cut Oil Refining Energy Use by Nearly a Third

One of the technology's biggest advantages is that refineries would not necessarily need to replace their existing equipment to use it.

The membrane could instead be installed as a modular filtration system that processes crude oil before it enters conventional distillation equipment. This would reduce the amount of work required during the heating and separation stages while allowing facilities to continue using much of their current infrastructure.

Computer simulations suggest that incorporating the membrane into the refining process could deliver substantial improvements. Energy consumption could fall by 31.6%, while carbon dioxide emissions could decrease by 37.6%. The same calculations projected a 20.7% reduction in cooling water consumption and a 36% decrease in operating costs.

The potential environmental benefits could be considerable if the technology were adopted widely.

Researchers estimate that implementing the system throughout Korea's refining and petrochemical industries could prevent approximately 10 million tonnes of greenhouse gas emissions each year. That is roughly equivalent to the annual emissions produced by four million vehicles powered by internal combustion engines.

These savings are projections based on process simulations rather than reductions already demonstrated across operating refineries. Nevertheless, the findings suggest that membrane filtration could become a practical way to improve the efficiency of existing facilities.

Although crude oil separation was the main focus of the research, the same technology could eventually be useful in several other industries.

One potential application involves treating pyrolysis oil produced when waste plastics are broken down for recycling. The membranes could also help recover solvents used in battery manufacturing, purify pharmaceutical compounds, and improve biofuel production.

The broader opportunity lies in using complex liquid mixtures to help form the tiny filtration channels needed to separate their components. This approach could provide a more affordable and versatile alternative to conventional membranes that require precisely manufactured surface coatings.

Professor Dong-Yeun Koh of KAIST said, "This study reveals a new scientific principle in which a membrane interacts with a complex mixture and spontaneously forms its own separation channels. Working with real crude oil supplied by HD Hyundai Oilbank allowed us to validate the technology under conditions relevant to industrial operation."

The use of actual crude oil was an important part of the research because it allowed the team to examine how the membrane performed with the complicated mixture of hydrocarbons found in industrial feedstocks.

Before the technology can be deployed more widely, the researchers plan to improve membrane production at larger scales and establish its reliability during extended operation.

Professor Jae W. Lee of KAIST, a co-corresponding author of the study, added, "By advancing large-area membrane modularization and long-term operational reliability, we hope to broaden the adoption of membrane-based processes throughout the refining and petrochemical industries."

Dr. Jihoon Choi and Dr. Hyeokjun Seo of KAIST, the study's co-first authors, said, "Our goal is to precisely control this spontaneous pore-constriction phenomenon and develop it into a membrane platform applicable to the entire refining process. We also aim to expand the technology to plastic recycling, biofuel purification, and other sustainable chemical processes that support carbon neutrality."

The research received support from Korea's Ministry of Science and ICT through the Basic Research Program for Outstanding Early-Career Researchers and the Engineering Research Center (ERC) Program.

The new contracts aim to pave the way for a permanent moon base.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. — NASA is pushing ahead with its plan to build a moon base for astronauts by 2032, with the agency unveiling up to $10 billion in contracts to launch and deliver cargo to the moon and other efforts on Saturday (Nov. 7).

The NASA announcement, revealed here during the space agency's "Max Power" air show event at Kennedy Space Center, included plans for a new $10 billion Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) framework, dubbed CLPS 2, about$1.3 billion in funding for the agency's Venture-Class Acquisition of Dedicated and Rideshare (VADR) program, and the nuclear-powered "PROMISE" rover on the moon.

The announcements mark another step in NASA's effort to establish infrastructure on the moon before Artemis astronauts return to its surface, including a rover and other cargo and research elements.

"Under the current CLPS contract, it's all all or nothing, which might be fine if you're only doing one or two of those [missions] per year," NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman told Space.com during a press conference on Saturday. "But when you're trying to scale up to what we're talking about today, you want to have the flexibility to move pieces around."

NASA selected eight companies to compete for the new CLPS 2 missions under the framework: Blue Origin, Firefly Aerospace, Intuitive Machines, ispace-U.S., Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, SpaceX and Voyager Technologies.

The contracts for the 10-year CLPS 2 architecture carry a combined maximum value of $10 billion, rather than $10 billion in immediately awarded missions. NASA also increased the ceiling of its existing CLPS contract from $2.6 billion to $4.2 billion to support the agency's "Phase One" Moon Base objectives.

NASA is also following through on a promise Isaacman made in June, when he proposed repurposing an engineering model of the Perseverance and Curiosity Mars rovers (essentially an Earth-based twin) as a mission-ready rover to send to the moon. That rover, called PROMISE (short for "Polar Rover for Observation, Mapping, and In-Situ Exploration"), is a nuclear-powered robot intended to explore the lunar south pole beginning in late 2028.

The autonomous rover will carry a drill and scientific instruments to search for volatiles and water ice on the lunar surface. NASA awarded Blue Origin a $94 million base contract, with an additional $140 million option period based on performance, to deliver PROMISE to the lunar surface aboard its Blue Moon Mark 1 lander.

In addition to that contract for Blue Origin, NASA awarded six launch and orbital transportation task orders worth a total of approximately $1.3 billion to Arrow Science and Technology, Blue Origin and Impulse Space under its Venture-Class Acquisition of Dedicated and Rideshare (VADR) program.

The missions will demonstrate commercial launch and orbital transportation capabilities, including cargo transfers between Earth and lunar orbits, navigation tests with the CAPSTONE 2 spacecraft and lunar scouting with "MoonFall" drones. Blue Origin, SpaceX and Relativity Space will provide launch support with their New Glenn, Falcon 9 and Terran R rockets, respectively.

Under a separate lunar logistics contract, NASA selected SpaceX to launch communications satellites aboard its Starship megarocket in 2028, helping to establish a future lunar communications network with spacecraft similar to the company's Starlink spacecraft.

NASA also awarded contracts to Honeybee Robotics, Redwire and Yank Technologies to develop components for a lunar power and communications tower, known as miniCAST.

The announcements support NASA's Phase One Moon Base strategy, which is scheduled to extend through 2029 and focuses on robotic exploration, infrastructure demonstrations and commercial deliveries. Phase Two, which runs from 2029 to 2032, will continue to build out infrastructure for the base, which will get up and running during Phase 3.

Josh Dinner is Space.com's Spaceflight Staff Writer and a photographer with a passion for science and exploration. He has worked the space beat since 2016, covering the evolution of NASA's commercial spaceflight partnerships and crewed missions, planetary science missions, the Artemis program and humanity's return to the moon. He also enjoys building 1:144-scale model rockets and spacecraft. Find some of Josh's launch photography on Instagram, and follow him on X, where he mostly posts in haiku.

#727. AI helps Stanford scientists discover a “natural Ozempic” with a surprising advantage

Scientists at Stanford Medicine have identified a naturally occurring molecule that could lead to a new generation of weight loss medications. Early animal experiments suggest that it can suppress appetite and promote fat loss much like semaglutide, the active ingredient in Ozempic, while potentially avoiding some of the drug's troublesome side effects.

The molecule, known as BRP, works differently from existing treatments. Rather than affecting several organs throughout the body, it appears to act more selectively on a part of the brain responsible for controlling hunger and metabolism. This more focused approach could eventually help people lose weight without experiencing problems such as nausea, constipation, or substantial muscle loss.

Researchers discovered BRP with the help of artificial intelligence, which allowed them to search through thousands of possible biological compounds. The findings were promising enough that the scientists began preparing for the next major step: determining whether the molecule is safe and effective in humans.

"The receptors targeted by semaglutide are found in the brain but also in the gut, pancreas and other tissues," said assistant professor of pathology Katrin Svensson, PhD. "That's why Ozempic has widespread effects including slowing the movement of food through the digestive tract and lowering blood sugar levels. In contrast, BRP appears to act specifically in the hypothalamus, which controls appetite and metabolism."

The hypothalamus is a small but essential region deep within the brain. Among its many responsibilities, it helps regulate hunger, energy use, body temperature, and other functions needed to maintain the body's internal balance. Because it plays such a central role in appetite, it is an important target for researchers developing obesity treatments.

Semaglutide works by imitating a hormone called glucagon-like peptide 1, or GLP-1. This hormone helps regulate blood sugar and signals that influence hunger and feelings of fullness. However, GLP-1 receptors are distributed throughout several parts of the body, which helps explain why medications that activate them can produce effects beyond appetite suppression.

BRP appears to take another route. Although it influences some of the same broad metabolic functions as semaglutide, it activates different populations of brain cells. Scientists believe this distinction could make it possible to control hunger more precisely while reducing unwanted effects elsewhere in the body.

Svensson, who served as senior author of the study, published in Nature, has also cofounded a company to advance BRP toward human clinical trials. The research was led by senior research scientist Laetitia Coassolo, PhD.

How Artificial Intelligence Uncovered a Hidden Molecule

Finding BRP required solving a problem that has long complicated the search for new hormones. The human body produces enormous numbers of small protein fragments, but only a fraction have important biological functions. Identifying the ones that influence appetite or metabolism can be extremely difficult.

Many hormones begin as larger, inactive proteins known as prohormones. Specialized enzymes cut these proteins into smaller pieces called peptides. Some of those peptides become chemical messengers that help coordinate processes such as energy metabolism, appetite, and organ function.

A single prohormone can be cut in several different places, potentially producing numerous peptides with distinct effects. The challenge is determining which fragments are biologically useful and which are simply leftovers from normal protein processing. The important peptide hormones (which are relatively rare) can be difficult to distinguish from the much larger collection of ordinary protein fragments.

Traditional approaches often involve extracting proteins from biological tissues and analyzing them with techniques such as mass spectrometry. This method identifies molecules by measuring characteristics related to their mass, but the sheer number of possible peptides makes searching for new hormones a demanding process.

The Stanford team decided to approach the problem differently. They concentrated on an enzyme called prohormone convertase 1/3, which cuts prohormones at particular amino acid sequences and has previously been linked to human obesity. Amino acids are the molecular building blocks of proteins, and their arrangement helps determine where enzymes can cut them.

One of the hormones produced through this process is GLP-1, the same hormone whose effects semaglutide mimics. The researchers reasoned that other peptides generated through similar processing might also help regulate appetite and energy use.

AI Searches 20,000 Human Genes for New Hormones

To accelerate the search, the scientists created a computer algorithm called Peptide Predictor. Instead of physically isolating and examining hundreds of thousands of peptides, the program analyzed the roughly 20,000 genes that encode human proteins, looking for sequences where the enzyme was likely to make cuts.

The team then refined the results by concentrating on genes associated with proteins released outside cells, a common characteristic of hormones. They also required each candidate protein to contain at least four potential cutting sites.

These filters reduced an enormous collection of possibilities to 373 prohormones, making experimental testing much more practical.

"The algorithm was absolutely key to our findings," Svensson said.

Peptide Predictor estimated that the enzyme could produce 2,683 distinct peptides from those 373 proteins. From this collection, Svensson and Coassolo selected candidates that appeared particularly likely to influence brain activity.

The researchers eventually tested 100 peptides, including GLP-1, using nerve cells grown in the laboratory. Their goal was to find substances capable of stimulating neuronal activity, an early indication that a peptide might influence important brain processes.

A Tiny Peptide Produces a Surprising Result

GLP-1 performed strongly in the laboratory tests, increasing neuronal activity to three times the level observed in untreated control cells.

One previously unrecognized peptide, however, produced an even more striking response. Consisting of just 12 amino acids, it increased neuronal activity tenfold compared with the controls.

The researchers named the molecule BRP after the larger protein from which it originates, BPM/retinoic acid inducible neural specific 2, or BRINP2 (BRINP2-related-peptide).

That unusually powerful response made BRP a promising candidate for further investigation. The next question was whether stimulating laboratory-grown brain cells would translate into meaningful changes in appetite and body weight in living animals.

Food Intake Drops by Up to 50% in Animal Experiments

The team tested BRP in lean mice and minipigs (which more closely mirror human metabolism and eating patterns than mice do). Before the animals were fed, researchers administered BRP through an injection into the muscle.

The results were striking. During the following hour, the treated animals consumed up to 50% less food than expected, suggesting that BRP could strongly influence hunger.

The scientists then examined whether repeated treatment could produce sustained changes in body weight. Obese mice received daily BRP injections for 14 days. By the end of the experiment, the treated mice had lost an average of 3 grams, while untreated control mice had gained approximately 3 grams.

Importantly, nearly all the weight lost by the BRP-treated mice came from body fat rather than muscle. Preserving muscle is an important goal in obesity treatment because muscle tissue supports strength, mobility, and metabolic health.

The treated animals also showed improvements in glucose and insulin tolerance. These measurements reflect how effectively the body handles sugar and responds to insulin, the hormone that helps move glucose from the bloodstream into cells.

Together, the findings suggest that BRP may influence both appetite and metabolic health, although it remains unknown whether people would experience comparable benefits.

Could BRP Avoid Common Ozempic Side Effects?

One of the most intriguing aspects of the discovery is the possibility that BRP could provide weight loss benefits while avoiding some unwanted effects associated with semaglutide and similar medications.

To investigate potential side effects, the researchers monitored the behavior and physical responses of the treated mice and pigs. They found no significant differences in movement, water consumption, anxiety-related behavior, or fecal output compared with control animals.

The absence of changes in fecal production was particularly interesting because constipation is a known side effect of medications such as Ozempic. The experiments also showed that BRP promoted fat loss without the substantial muscle loss that can accompany some weight reduction treatments.

Nausea is another common concern with existing GLP-1 medications, although animal experiments cannot fully establish whether BRP would prevent that symptom in people. Human testing will be essential to determine the molecule's actual side effect profile.

Additional investigations into brain activity and other physiological responses reinforced the idea that BRP works differently from semaglutide. The peptide activated distinct neuronal and metabolic pathways rather than simply copying the effects of GLP-1.

This difference may explain why the researchers observed strong appetite suppression without several of the behavioral and digestive changes they were monitoring.

What Comes Next for the Potential Ozempic Alternative?

Despite the encouraging findings, BRP is still at an early stage of development. Researchers need to understand more about exactly how the molecule communicates with cells and how its effects might be sustained over longer periods.

One priority is identifying the cell surface receptors that recognize BRP. Receptors are specialized proteins that respond to particular chemical signals, allowing cells to detect messages and trigger appropriate biological responses. Determining which receptors BRP activates could help explain its effects on hunger and metabolism.

The team also wants to investigate ways of extending the molecule's activity inside the body. Peptides can be broken down relatively quickly, potentially requiring frequent injections. A longer-lasting version of BRP could make treatment more convenient if it eventually proves effective in people.

The ultimate challenge will be establishing whether its apparent advantages in animals translate into meaningful benefits for patients. Clinical trials will need to evaluate its safety, effectiveness, appropriate dosage, and potential side effects before it could become a practical obesity treatment.

"The lack of effective drugs to treat obesity in humans has been a problem for decades," Svensson said. "Nothing we've tested before has compared to semaglutide's ability to decrease appetite and body weight. We are very eager to learn if it is safe and effective in humans."

Scientists from the University of California, Berkeley; the University of Minnesota; and the University of British Columbia also participated in the research.

Financial support came from the National Institutes of Health (grants R01DK125260, P30DK116074, K99AR081618 and GM113854), the SPARK Translational Research Program at Stanford, Stanford Bio-X, the Stanford Maternal and Child Health Research Institute, the American Heart Association, a Stanford Medicine Dean's Fellowship Award, the Carlsberg Foundation, and the Wu Tsai Human Performance Alliance.

Svensson and Coassolo are named inventors on patents involving the use of BRP peptides to treat metabolic disorders. Svensson is also a cofounder of Merrifield Therapeutics.

#725. After Wasserman’s Exit, The Team Forms New Board of Directors

The 11-member board is comprised of leaders across the Mike Watts-led sports, music and representation giant as the rebranded firm charts its next chapter under Providence Equity Partners.

As it looks to chart a path away from its namesake founder, the Hollywood representation powerhouse The Team is installing a new board of directors stocked with leaders from key constituencies across the company.

The Westwood-based firm, formerly known as Wasserman, unveiled an 11-person board on Tuesday comprised of in-house exec members. Mike Watts, the CEO who took the helm amid founder Casey Wasserman’s tumultuous exit tied to an artist exodus in February, will serve on the board.

So too will Jon Liebman, the chief of Brillstein Entertainment Partners, the pioneering management and production firm that was acquired by Wasserman three years ago in a major expansion.

Kevin Shivers, who was promoted in April to co-president of music as part of the stabilization of that department (which had been bulked up through the acquisition of Paradigm’s roster five years ago), is also taking a seat on the board.

Leaders like Elizabeth Lindsey, who oversees the brands and properties business, Jason Ranne, who leads talent representation, the U.K.-based international chief Matthew Vandrau and CFO Elena Rochelli were also named to the board, as were C-suiters Davis Noell, Greg Brown and Scott Marimow.

Providence Equity Partners, the majority investor in The Team which formally bought out Wasserman’s interest after a bidding process over the summer, added its SVP Ahana Maken to the board and says that it will “name additional external board members in the coming months.” The firm has been invested in the company since 2022 when it took the place of prior backers RedBird Capital and Madrone Capital Partners.

The Team is one of the biggest players in the fast-growing sports representation space, along with CAA. And it has a large music roster that is being rebuilt after a slew of departures made waves in that space when Wasserman was linked to Ghislaine Maxwell over decades-old flirtatious emails unearthed by the Department of Justice in January.

The company, originally founded in 2002, has snapped up many multiple boutique agencies and had 4,000 employees as of earlier this year. Its latest acquisition was unveiled just last month, when it bought Outreach Talent Group, co-founded by Emilio Arciniega, which has its main base in London.

#724. MIT scientists break a 20-year rule and unlock never-before-seen crystal structures

Scientists have spent decades trying to control how tiny particles connect to form advanced materials. Now, researchers at MIT and their collaborators have discovered that doing the exact opposite of what was previously believed necessary can produce remarkable results.

Instead of relying on rigid molecular connections to hold nanoparticles in carefully planned arrangements, the team developed extremely flexible connectors that bend and adjust as particles come together. This unexpected strategy gives scientists a new way to control how nanoparticles organize themselves, allowing them to create crystal structures that have never been observed before.

The discovery could help overcome a major obstacle in materials science and open new possibilities for creating substances with precisely engineered properties. Potential applications include electronics, medicine, energy technologies, agriculture, and chemical manufacturing.

The findings, described in a paper that will appear in Nature Materials, demonstrate how the flexibility and electrical charges of molecular connectors can determine the structures that nanoparticles form.

MIT Researchers Challenge 20 Years of Materials Science

"People are interested in nanoparticle superlattices because of the promise of building designer materials where you have more say in what types of structures they can actually build into," says Rob Macfarlane, the Richard P. Simmons (1953) Professor in Metallurgy in MIT's Department of Materials Science and Engineering. "This is a new approach in nanoparticle assembly that hasn't been investigated before. It's exciting to have a new tool that is so counterintuitive. It's the exact opposite of what the dogma has been for 20 years: that you need to make connector ligands rigid, and any deviation causes assembly to fail. We showed if you just crank it all the way to the opposite extreme, it works just as well."

The research team also included MIT PhD candidate Nicholas Sbalbi, University of Delaware doctoral student Stephen Kronenberger, MIT undergraduate Hana Shinzawa, Matthew Ye PhD '26, and Arthi Jayaraman, a former professor at the University of Delaware.

At the heart of the discovery is a basic principle of materials science: The way a material's smallest components are arranged determines how that material behaves.

"That means if you know what your building blocks are and how they're arranged, you can explain what properties materials have," Macfarlane says. "Controlling that is how you make materials that have new properties."

This principle is especially important when working with nanoparticles, which are extremely small pieces of matter whose shapes, sizes, and properties can be adjusted for different purposes. Scientists already use individual nanoparticles in technologies involving drug delivery, energy storage, computing, and sensors.

But turning these tiny building blocks into larger, organized materials presents a difficult challenge.

Why Nanoparticles Are So Difficult to Control

One of the biggest obstacles is controlling how nanoparticles attach to one another. Scientists need to determine not only how many neighboring particles each nanoparticle connects with, but also the directions in which those connections form.

Without that control, nanoparticles tend to assemble into tightly packed arrangements that restrict the variety of structures researchers can produce. This limits their ability to create materials with unusual or specialized properties.

Researchers have traditionally approached the problem in two ways. One strategy involves changing the shapes of nanoparticles to influence how they fit together. Another involves modifying specific areas of their surfaces so that only certain regions attract neighboring particles.

In effect, scientists attempt to control where the particles stick to one another, much like designing puzzle pieces that can connect only in particular positions.

Although these methods can produce useful structures, they are often complicated, highly specialized, and difficult to adapt for large-scale production.

"The challenge with both of those approaches is they're difficult to do synthetically as we make the particles," Macfarlane explains. "The methods for defining stickiness that have been developed are always bespoke: They work for one material, at one size scale, in one condition. It's good for studying, but you can't do much with it."

Both strategies also depend on molecular connectors called ligands. These molecules attach to the surfaces of nanoparticles and help link neighboring particles together.

Traditionally, researchers have tried to make these ligands rigid so the connections remain at carefully controlled angles. This helps maintain a desired arrangement, but it also restricts the types of structures that can form and the functions they can perform.

The MIT team decided to explore a radically different possibility.

A Surprising Discovery About Flexible Molecular Bonds

Rather than forcing molecular connectors to remain in fixed positions, the researchers wondered whether giving them almost complete freedom to bend could offer an entirely new form of control.

"We thought, 'Let's do the exact opposite: make the bonds so flexible it doesn't matter what direction they're initially pointing.' The ligands can then reorganize as the particles come together, and that reorganization itself limits how many neighbors each particle can bind," Macfarlane says.

The idea reverses the usual approach to nanoparticle assembly. Instead of controlling the orientation of every connection in advance, the scientists allow the connectors to adjust naturally as the particles interact.

Macfarlane's laboratory has spent years developing ways to construct different types of nanoparticles using attached polymer chains. Polymers are large molecules made of repeating smaller units, and their flexibility makes them useful for creating adjustable molecular connections.

For the new system, the team equipped nanoparticles with highly flexible ligands that carry electrical charges at their ends. Some have positive charges, while others have negative charges.

Because opposite electrical charges attract, the connector molecules naturally bend toward partners with the opposite charge. This attraction helps the nanoparticles join together, while the flexibility of the connectors influences how many connections each particle can make.

"The idea is, instead of defining a specific direction the bonds are going to occur in with complicated synthesis methods, we just said, 'The bonds are going to be as flexible as they want to be, and they'll spontaneously go to whatever valency is going to maximize bond stability,'" Macfarlane says.

In this context, valency refers to the number of connections a nanoparticle forms with its neighbors. By allowing the connectors to move freely, the researchers found that the system could naturally settle into stable arrangements without requiring every connection to be designed beforehand.

Scientists Create Crystal Structures Never Seen Before

Experiments led by Sbalbi demonstrated that the researchers could adjust the connections between nanoparticles by changing two relatively straightforward characteristics: the sizes of the particles and the lengths of their flexible molecular chains.

These adjustments altered how the particles assembled, giving the team control over the number of neighboring particles each one could connect with.

Most importantly, the researchers used this method to produce previously unseen crystal structures.

Crystals are materials whose building blocks form organized, repeating patterns. In this case, the repeating arrangements are made from nanoparticles rather than individual atoms or small molecules. Such ordered nanoparticle networks are often called superlattices.

By reducing the number of connections between neighboring particles, the team was able to create more open arrangements instead of the densely packed structures that commonly form during nanoparticle assembly.

"Without having to predesign where the particles connect or what their shapes are, we can control the number of bonds each particle has," Macfarlane explains. "The amount of flexibility of the polymer dictates how many bonds it has. It allows us to lower the number of bonds each particle has and make lattices we have never seen before."

The results suggest that molecular flexibility, once viewed as an obstacle to precise nanoparticle assembly, can instead become a powerful tool for engineering new material structures.

A New Path Toward Customizable Designer Materials

The researchers believe their method could bring scientists closer to a long-sought goal in materials science: choosing the properties of individual nanoparticles independently of the larger structures into which they assemble.

Ideally, scientists could select nanoparticles for their electrical, optical, chemical, or other useful characteristics and then organize those particles into whatever arrangement best serves a particular application.

In practice, however, existing assembly methods have made that level of flexibility difficult to achieve.

"We in the nanoparticle assembly community talk about having completely independent control over what your particle is and what assembly it goes into," Macfarlane says. "In theory, that should be the case. In reality, it absolutely has not been."

The new approach could help close that gap. Because the researchers can influence nanoparticle arrangements through the flexibility of their connectors and the attraction between electrical charges, they may be able to create a wider variety of structures without the complicated manufacturing techniques required by traditional methods.

The team also sees the discovery as a promising route toward producing customizable materials at larger scales, potentially helping move nanoparticle technologies beyond laboratory experiments and into practical use.

Potential Applications in Electronics, Medicine, and Energy

The ability to build more open and varied nanoparticle structures could prove particularly valuable for developing advanced materials.

In photonics, which involves controlling and manipulating light, precisely organized nanoparticles could help researchers engineer materials with specialized optical properties. In chemical catalysis, where substances accelerate chemical reactions, new particle arrangements could create opportunities to improve the way catalysts operate.

The approach may also support future developments in medicine, agriculture, electronics, and energy technologies.

A major advantage is that nanoparticles can already possess a wide range of desirable properties. By controlling how those particles come together, scientists may be able to combine their individual capabilities in new ways.

"Nanoparticle superlattices offer a way to create designer materials where your building blocks have all sort sorts of unique properties," Macfarlane says. "But just densely packing these nanoparticles together limits your applications. This offers a way to get less dense formations of nanoparticles, and that's where a lot of the interesting applications are."

Although further development will be needed to translate the method into commercial technologies, the discovery establishes molecular flexibility as a new strategy for creating materials with tailored structures.

Instead of treating bending molecular connections as a problem to eliminate, scientists may now be able to use that flexibility to unlock arrangements that rigid designs could not easily achieve.

The research received partial support from the National Science Foundation, the Department of Energy, the U.S. Army, and the U.S. Navy.

CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. — NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman knows how to make an entrance. Under the bright afternoon sun on Saturday (Nov. 7), Isaacman plummeted through the air above 10,000 onlookers, skydiving into the agency's air show MAX POWER.

MAX POWER overtook NASA's Kennedy Space Center here over the weekend, combining aeronautics and aerospace in a massive public air show, the first of its kind for the space agency. A mix of astronauts, fighter jet displays and new technology on display, the spectacle is a lot space-ier than a traditional air show, and Isaacman made sure to really showcase this merging of worlds. A pilot and private astronaut, Jared Isaacman is no stranger to the skies, and immediately after landing back on solid ground he jumped right back up and took to the event's main stage to greet an excited crowd.

"Going into this job, I I knew we had to do something like this," Isaacman said after landing and taking the stage. "We knew on our nation's 250th birthday, we had to open up [the] Kennedy Space Center the year that we returned our astronauts to the lunar environment and put on a little bit of a show."

This mirrorless Canon has specs that make it one of the best cameras available right now, with impressive features and functionality, including a 45MP sensor and excellent high-ISO handling.

Check our in-depth Canon R5 Mark II review.

From thousands of feet above a crowd holding their breath, Isaacman jumped out of a plane alongside members of Skydive Chicago and other notable individuals, including Montana senator Tim Sheehy (R-Montana) and former U.S. Air Force Thunderbird pilot Shawn Gustoson.

One by one, tiny white parachutes popped up in the sky above, which continued to grow in size as the skydivers neared the ground. And before we knew it, Isaacman was gracefully touching down just behind the air show's main stage, landing to the sound of cheers from the eager audience.

In addition to serving in his role as NASA Administrator, Isaacman is an entrepreneur, commercial astronaut and pilot. Known in flight by his callsign "Rook" which he was given during fighter jet training, Isaacman has so far logged over 8,000 flight hours. In 2009, he broke the world record for fastest trip around the world in a light jet (he made the trip in 61 hours, 51 minutes and 15 seconds) and is flight-qualified in a number of military jet aircraft. He also financed and flew on two private orbital space missions on a SpaceX Dragon, Inspiration4 and Polaris Dawn, performing the world's first private spacewalk on the latter misison.

Before jumping out of a plane and careening through the air on Saturday as part of this celebratory stunt, Isaacman was actually flying overhead in not one, but two different fighter jets.

First, he flew an F-5, a lightweight supersonic fighter jet, and just a short while later, Isaacman flew a MiG-29, a twin-engine supersonic fighter jet, over the crowd of excited air show attendees. And the fun didn't stop with this skydive, as Isaacman took to the skies once again, flying over the event in fighter jets on Sunday.

This weekend's MAX POWER events are not a one-time-only celebration of aviation and aerospace at NASA. Earlier in the weekend, the agency announced that in 2028, a week-long event called CAPEWEEK will return to the Kennedy Space Center, promising a next-level showcase of air and space innovation and spectacle.

Isaacman and NASA astronauts presented President Donald Trump, who was onhand for the ceremony, with a gold plaque in his honor that will be installed at the Kennedy Space Center's Shuttle Landing Facility runway in time for the CAPEWEEK in 2028.

"What you are seeing today again, imagine March 2028," Isaacman said of the future. "It's going to be 10x bigger. I mean, not just the the fighter aircraft you're seeing, but displays of aerospace-related hardware, rovers, landers. We're going to bring commercial airliners in here ... I would bet on this, the next new Grand Airliner will be announced here."

"That kind of ambition is exactly that you should expect from your space agency," he added. "I promise you, there'll be more to come."

#722. From ‘Dil Se’ to ‘Ramayana’: How Indian Cinema Shattered the U.K., Ireland Box Office Glass Ceiling

When Mani Ratnam’s romantic thriller “Dil Se..” debuted in August 1998, it achieved what was then considered unthinkable for South Asian cinema: entering the official U.K. and Ireland top 10 box office chart at No. 8. Powered by Shah Rukh Khan’s burgeoning overseas stardom and A.R. Rahman’s ubiquitous soundtrack, the film proved that Indian releases could cut through mainstream British multiplexes on limited screens.

That watershed moment initiated a 28-year ascent across Bollywood and South Indian regional industries, culminating this weekend when Sony Pictures’ mythological epic “Ramayana: Rise of a Legend” debuted at No. 1 with £2.1 million ($2.8 million) including previews, officially claiming the territory’s box office summit. Related Stories Taylor Swift, Inducted Into Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame, Says 'There Is No Music Community Like This Music Community. I Know, I Checked All the Communities' Taylor Swift and Karlie Kloss Reunite at Travis Kelce’s Chiefs Game Against Jets

Before “Dil Se..,” Indian cinema’s U.K. and Ireland footprint was largely confined to single screens and community halls in South Asian diaspora hubs such as Southall, Wembley, Leicester and Birmingham. While films like “Hum Aapke Hain Koun..!” (1994) and “Dilwale Dulhania Le Jayenge” (1995) generated significant receipts – eventually crossing the £1 million ($1.6 million) mark over prolonged runs – they operated in an isolated distribution ecosystem outside mainstream computerized reporting.

The breakthrough of “Dil Se..” transformed the market landscape. Just two months later, Karan Johar’s directorial debut “Kuch Kuch Hota Hai” built on that foundation, bowing inside the top 10 and amassing £1.7 million ($3 million). In 2001, Johar’s multi-starrer “Kabhi Khushi Kabhie Gham…” rewrote the record books, reaching No. 3 with £473,255 ($681,000) in its first week from just 41 screens and finishing its run with nearly £2.5 million ($3.6 million). Over the next decade, a string of major Bollywood releases – including Sanjay Leela Bhansali’s “Devdas” (2002), Yash Chopra’s “Veer-Zaara” (2004) and Johar’s “Kabhi Alvida Naa Kehna” (2006) – cemented Hindi-language cinema as a reliable weekend fixture in the U.K. top 10.

The threshold moved higher in 2010 when 20th Century Fox released Karan Johar’s “My Name Is Khan,” starring Shah Rukh Khan and Kajol, on 91 screens. The drama debuted at No. 6 with £936,000 ($1.4 million) and concluded with £2.6 million ($4.1 million). Three years later, Aamir Khan’s action franchise entry “Dhoom 3” (2013) raised the bar further, bowing with £884,567 ($1.4 million) and becoming the first Indian film to cross £2.7 million ($4.4 million) in the territory. Aamir Khan continued to push commercial frontiers with “PK” (2014), which grossed £2.3 million ($3.7 million), and “Dangal” (2016), which delivered £2.5 million ($3.2 million), alongside Salman Khan’s “Bajrangi Bhaijaan” (2015), which reached £2.6 million ($4.1 million).

Yet for all of Bollywood’s commercial muscle, an unyielding glass ceiling remained: chart positions consistently hovered between No. 3 and No. 10 against Hollywood tentpoles. Furthermore, South Indian cinema remained hindered by fragmented distribution.

That began to shift in April 2017 with S.S. Rajamouli’s “Baahubali 2: The Conclusion,” starring Prabhas. The film released across several languages and crossed £1 million ($1.3 million) in the territory within 10 days. However, fragmented reporting hindered its peak chart placement. The official chart, compiled by Comscore, listed each language version separately: the Hindi-language version opened at No. 6 with £221,452 ($286,000) from 50 sites and the Tamil-language version at No. 9 with £194,522 ($251,000) from 39 sites, while the Malayalam and Telugu-language versions charted lower. Even combined, its roughly £455,000 ($587,000) would have placed it only No. 6, behind “Their Finest” (£630,544; $813,000) and far below the £13.1 million ($16.9 million) bow of “Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2.”

The ceiling truly began to crack when Rajamouli’s “RRR” landed in March 2022. Driven by massive event demand, the Telugu epic debuted at No. 2 with £650,204 ($858,000) from 160 locations, including previews, held off from the summit only by Warner Bros.’ “The Batman.”

The subsequent wave of pan-Indian spectacle gradually united reporting streams and brought Southern regional industries into the mainstream multiplex fold. Mani Ratnam’s Tamil historical epic “Ponniyin Selvan: I” (2022) delivered a £745,000 ($834,000) opening weekend across 119 U.K. sites, charting at No. 5 and finishing with £1.2 million ($1.3 million). In March 2024, Blessy’s survival drama “Aadujeevitham – The Goat Life,” starring Prithviraj Sukumaran, set benchmarks for Malayalam cinema, debuting at No. 5 with £556,514 ($702,000) and grossing some £717,000 ($903,000) across its run. That summer, Nag Ashwin’s sci-fi epic “Kalki 2898 AD,” also starring Prabhas, released by Dreamz Entertainment across 450 U.K. sites, opened at No. 3 with £886,366 ($1.1 million) and went on to pass £1.5 million ($1.9 million).

Shah Rukh Khan starrers matched the historic No. 2 benchmark of “RRR” twice in 2023. In January, Siddharth Anand’s spy thriller “Pathaan” opened at No. 2 with a £1.4 million ($1.74 million) three-day weekend (reaching £1.97 million, or $2.44 million, over five days), behind James Cameron’s holdover “Avatar: The Way of Water,” on its way to a then-record U.K. total of £4.38 million ($5.4 million). In September 2023, Atlee’s action thriller “Jawan” mirrored the feat, debuting at No. 2 with £1.35 million ($1.67 million). Ranbir Kapoor’s violent action drama “Animal” (2023) opened lower, at No. 6 with £719,000 ($906,000), but legged out to £2.37 million ($3 million).

In March this year, Aditya Dhar’s spy sequel “Dhurandhar: The Revenge” became the fourth Indian film to open at No. 2, with a then-record £1.6 million ($2.1 million) Friday-to-Sunday weekend, or £2.1 million ($2.8 million) including previews. It went on to overtake “Pathaan” as the territory’s highest-grossing Indian release, with more than £4.4 million ($5.9 million).

South Indian cinema hit its own high-water mark in October this year, when Nelson Dilipkumar’s Tamil-language action sequel “Jailer 2,” starring Rajinikanth, opened at No. 3 with £1.1 million ($1.5 million) from just 228 sites, the highest site average of the weekend. Within 10 days, it had become the highest-grossing Tamil film in the territory with £1.6 million ($2.1 million).

Until this week, No. 2 remained the undisputed ceiling for Indian cinema in the territory.

That boundary fell with “Ramayana: Rise of a Legend.” Directed by Nitesh Tiwari (“Dangal”) and produced by Namit Malhotra’s Prime Focus Studios and DNEG in association with Yash’s Monster Mind Creations, the film is the first of a two-part adaptation of the Hindu epic. Ranbir Kapoor plays Rama, Yash plays the demon king Ravana and Sai Pallavi plays Sita, with Sunny Deol as Hanuman and Ravie Dubey as Lakshmana. The story pits the prince against the vengeful king and ends with Ravana’s abduction of Sita, stopping short of the war between them. Backed by a wide, format-heavy rollout across 364 sites that included premium 3D and large-format screens, the film’s £2.1 million ($2.8 million) debut – a new opening record for an Indian film in the territory – outstripped competing releases, including Disney’s “Wild Horse Nine” (£1.48 million; $1.97 million) at No. 2 and Anime Ltd.’s “Godzilla Minus Zero” (£1.3 million; $1.8 million) at No. 3.

From Mani Ratnam’s political romance sneaking into the lower rungs of the top 10 in 1998, through the trailblazing runs of “Baahubali 2,” “RRR,” “Pathaan” and “The Goat Life,” to a mythological tentpole conquering the weekend chart in 2026, Indian cinema has traveled from diaspora counterprogramming to the top of the U.K. and Ireland chart. However, the full-run numbers still lag well behind. The highest-grossing Indian release in the territory, “Dhurandhar: The Revenge,” has taken just over £4.4 million ($5.9 million), a fraction of what the biggest Hollywood and British releases earn. “Project Hail Mary,” which kept “Dhurandhar” off the top spot in March, passed £15 million ($20 million) in two weekends, while “Avatar: The Way of Water” was above £70 million ($86.8 million) by its seventh. “Ramayana” has broken the ceiling for one weekend. Breaking it over a full run is the next test.

#721. ‘Nobody Wants This’ Star Timothy Simons Reveals Biggest Season 3 Concern and Looks to Season 4: “They Burned One Another — So They’re Even”

The 'Veep' actor also opens up about his co-stars and creator weighing in on Adam Brody's Gaza comments, and how being on the Jewish show has shaped his own views on religion.

[This story contains spoilers from Nobody Wants This season two.]

When Timothy Simons and Justine Lupe found out that this would be such a big season for their Nobody Wants This duo Sasha and Morgan, respectively, Simons said he and his co-star had some key concerns.

“We are very limb-forward people. We have a lot of arms,” he tells The Hollywood Reporter with a laugh. “Even weeks before we left [to film the] New York [episode], I said to our director, ‘Hey, can we talk about the blocking for this? Because we just don’t want to look like muppets.'” Related Stories Movies 'Steps' Review: A Stellar Voice Cast Including Amanda Seyfried, Ali Wong and Bette Midler Gets Stuck in a Tortured Revisionist Fairy Tale TV 'Nobody Wants This' Stars Hint at Season 4 and Declare Timothy Simons "the Lead of the Show Now"

When it came time to film the seventh episode of season two, “Watch What Happens,” Simons said he and Lupe took the trust and responsibility of their story getting such a spotlight seriously. The result was a bottle episode that is getting rave reviews for taking Sasha and Morgan out of Los Angeles and landing them in a bed together, only to blow up their romance shortly after when Esther (Jackie Tohn), Sasha’s estranged wife, reveals she and Sasha also slept together. The finale leaves the trio, once again, in a love triangle. But it’s slightly different this time around.

“It’s a pretty mature choice for Sasha to be like, ‘This might be the right thing, but it’s the wrong time.’ I also think there was a fair amount of maturity in what Morgan did after years and years of not trying and running from things. So I don’t know which way it’s going to go,” he says of how season three ends, now that the hit Netflix series has been officially renewed for season four.

Below, the Veep actor shares his hopes for next season (the writers room has been up and running), and weighs in on co-star Adam Brody’s Gaza comments, how the show has shaped his views on religion and why Nobody Wants This is not likely to bring such conversations to the Roklov dinner table. “Adam and Erin are both immensely passionate about the views they’ve spoken to. I know they have spoken personally about it before. It’s always respectful,” he says.

So whose idea was it to dye your hair blonde for the season?

I had done it for fun for the Emmys a couple of years ago, when we were there with the show after the first season. All the writers saw it sort of separately and each individually had the idea to write that in. Then they all got together and realized they all had that same thought, so they wrote it in and I had to keep it.

Were you over being a blonde by the end of filming?

I actually loved it and thought it fit the vibe, because Sasha is going through something. Although I wasn’t going through something, I could definitely see how it would fit someone like Sasha going through something. And I will say, if you have hair as short and dark as mine, it requires more upkeep than you think and is a bit of a continuity nightmare. I didn’t get sick of it through the entire season; I really did like it. But after, I did get sick of the upkeep so I’m back to brunette. I’m rocking my real self now and it feels good.

When did you find out this was going to be such a big season for Sasha and Morgan (Justine Lupe)? Can you take me inside that conversation with your creator/showrunners when they first laid it out for you?

Justine and I went into the writers room. They had outlined the entire season and pitched it out to Netflix, and Netflix OK’d it. We do that every year — we sit down and they bring us through the broad strokes. We talk about it a lot and throw out ideas that they can either take or leave. So it was in the writers room early on when we found out.

We’re a 10-episode show and they told us that episode seven was going to be dedicated to just the two of us. As a performer, that feels incredible that they have that amount of trust in Justine and I to hand over responsibility of a full episode just to us. That is immensely flattering. I think we both had the same reaction. We took that seriously. We took that trust and responsibility seriously.

That episode is getting raves for being like a mini rom-com bottle episode. You and Justine are close friends. What was it like to play out Sasha and Morgan’s sexual tension, and eventually sleep together?

We’ve always had similar styles, or at least similar thought processes on performance, which I think is why we get along so well and have chemistry. We have a lot of mutual friends. There was a lot of trust in Justine, at least on my side, from very early on.

We are very limb-forward people. We’re very lanky. We have a lot of arms. (Laughs.) And we just didn’t want to look like muppets when we ended up kissing. So we talked a lot to our director, Richard Shepard, who is incredible. Even weeks before we left for New York I was like, “Hey, can we talk about the blocking for this? Because we just don’t want to look like muppets.”

Because the moment they kiss, if that moment doesn’t work, then none of it works. You built it all up to that. And if we look like muppets, it would undercut the whole thing. But it’s our jobs and we’re close, and we joked around about it a lot. But both of us are professionals about it.

Did you see the twist coming of Sasha and Esther (Jackie Tohn) reuniting?

I didn’t. I feel like hooking up with your ex is a thing that has happened to a lot of people. You can’t just all of a sudden shake off a 20-year relationship and not have that come up again. I didn’t necessarily see it coming, but that felt like something that does naturally happen sometimes. So it did take me by surprise a little bit. But in a good way. Conflict and confrontations are good for drama!

The finale ends unresolved about who he is going to pick, if anyone. Where would you say his heart lies by the end of the season?

I’ve mentioned this to Justine before. Justine is such an incredible performer and can access such an immense vulnerability — especially in that scene in the parking garage. There were times as an actor that I was like, “Can we just fix this for her so she doesn’t have to feel like this?!” But there was a fair amount of maturity that I didn’t even realize until I watched the season. It’s a pretty mature choice for him to be like, “This might be the right thing, but it’s the wrong time.” I don’t think he’s ever said that before. He very much went along with whatever anyone else wanted for him, and so I do think it was a mature choice for him to make to be like, “It seems like not the right thing in either direction.”

So I don’t know which way it’s going to go. But it does seem like he is a little bit like, “I have to back off of both of these things for a little bit.”

Do you think Morgan could be mature enough to get over being burned by Sasha, if he does want to pursue a relationship with her?

I also think there was a fair amount of maturity in what Morgan did after years and years of not trying and running from things. And being willing to take a risk that she’s never taken before and not half-assing anything. I feel like if she is taking steps in that direction, and there could be a world. Also, I would throw in that they kind of burned one another. She kind of burned him when she ran away and he kind of burned her when she said no. So they are still at an even point.

We heard the writers room has been up. Erin Foster was recently said on Dax Shepard’s podcast that they were writing a role for him. Have any ideas been shared with you yet? [Note: This interview occurred before the official season four renewal.]

I would absolutely love to do more of it. I’ve enjoyed the cast and crew and writers and directors of this show immensely. So doing more of it? I’m 100 percent in favor for. But I’m not being cagey when I tell you that I don’t have any idea what they’re talking about, because I haven’t gone in to do the sit down yet.

What decisions would you like to see Sasha making in season four?

The writers are always coming up with better things than me. I have my personal feelings, but they will always come up with better ideas. Either way, he and Esther reconciling… clearly, they do love one another. They built a life together, so you’d like to see them work through that. Maybe they slip back into old habits and all that work he did to put himself together a little bit more goes by the wayside.

And I love the idea of two weirdos like Sasha and Morgan finding each other and that working out, but maybe that’s too messy with the family. There are pros and cons on either side, so I’m interested to see what the writers come up with.

This season got a lot of attention for two things. First, because of the big endings for both Noah (Adam Brody) and Joanne (Kristen Bell), and you and Morgan. But also because of your creator Erin Foster and co-stars responding to Brody’s Gaza comments. Do you feel like there is a responsibility for your writers and cast to speak out because the show is a Jewish show? How do you feel about it, and how do you feel about being asked about it?

Adam and Erin are both immensely passionate about the views they’ve spoken to. And I do think the way Erin said it… they work together really well. I know they have spoken personally about it before. It’s always respectful, and that’s one of the great things about Adam is that he is kind and thoughtful and empathetic and will talk to anybody, even if their views don’t align with his, to try to fight for a safer world for everybody. That’s what’s underneath all of it.

Erin said the show is a love letter to Judaism. After playing a Jewish character on this show, how has that shaped or informed your views on Judaism?

I’ve never been a religious person. I didn’t grow up religious. I had an Irish-Catholic grandmother, but religion was not a huge part of my family or my life coming into the show. But I will say, my dad passed away recently…

Thank you. There was a moment when I got back to Los Angeles after the [funeral] service; we have neighbors who we’ve been good friends with since our kids were in kindergarten together, and they invited me to go to Shabbat at the temple they go to in our neighborhood. There’s a mourner’s circle [the Kaddish] and it was incredible to go to a temple and be welcomed in and be able to say my dad’s name out loud and a rabbi told me, “May his memory be a blessing.”

Even as a non-religious person — I’m certainly not a scholar — there are a lot of rituals surrounding death and mourning and grief that I have learned through this experience of learning more about Judaism that even if I am not religious, have given me a lot of comfort.

Shortly after my dad died, my college roommate died of brain cancer, so I’m in a mourner’s circle saying two names. You realize why religion has been around so long as a guide through moments of grief and to try to find some sense of comfort. That is something that, albeit, I did now know coming in[to this show]. There has been a lot of stuff I learned that has helped me in my day-to-day life because of this experience.

I’m really sorry about your friend and about your dad.

Thank you, I appreciate it. It’s been a little bit of a rough summer, but we’re working through it.

Nobody Wants This isn’t a political show. It’s a feel-good show. Have you had conversations with the writers about if the show would get more current as it goes, or is that not the ethos of the show? Will the extended Roklov family ever be arguing over the war at the dinner table?

Yeah, that has not been the language of this show so far, and I would also throw back to you that the writers always know better than me. If they want to find a way into that, [they will]. Just like I said before about a love triangle, they are going to know how to best attack it.

Your kids [14-year-old twins] love Nobody Wants This. When will you show them Veep?

I actually, for a very long time, had not appeared in a single project that they could have watched. (Laughs.) Now we are at a point where with some outliers, we can pretty much show them everything. We have a lot of movie nights as a family where we’ll show them Rear Window and Mad Max: Fury Road and John Wick. So I do think they are ready to watch Veep. However, there has to be a conversation about, “This is not language that you use in school or with teachers, or in any sort of important situation.”

Would you want to do a Veep revival, or is the real world still getting in the way of that?

Would I love to be in the room with all of those people again? The answer is 100 percent, yes. But we also live in a world that is un-satirizable. The show would be completely different and honestly, what are we going to do that’s dumber than what’s happening? We live in a world that’s beyond parody, so how could we possibly parody it? Would I love to work with those people again? That would be amazing. But I don’t know how it would fit.

I’m glad the show has stayed relevant and people still enjoy it and still see a reflection of the world now, even though we made it so long ago. It’s been six or seven years since it went off the air. That’s amazing. I would sacrifice a little bit of the longtail of the show if the world were a little bit less chaotic. I would really like for fewer people to tell me Veep was still relevant if the world was a little better.

Nobody Wants This season two is now streaming all episodes on Netflix.
